duca-pfg-financial.html:
In today’s business financing landscape, speed matters. Clients expect quick answers, deals move fast, and business consultants, accountants, and other centres of influence need lending partners who can keep opportunities moving.

That’s where DUCA Financial Services Credit Union Ltd. (DUCA) is making an impact.

Through its partnership with PFG Financial, DUCA is providing business consultants and accountants with access to responsive financing solutions, streamlined decision-making, and a Business Banking team focused on helping clients secure the capital they need to grow.

Like many successful partnerships, this one began with a simple conversation.

The two organizations first connected at the Canadian SME Small Business Show in May 2024. What started as networking quickly revealed a shared philosophy: put clients first, simplify the process, and focus on outcomes. That common ground laid the foundation for a partnership built on collaboration, communication, and results.

“At DUCA, we understand that business consultants and accountants need more than approvals, they need momentum,” says Robert Edwards, Senior Manager, Business Banking at DUCA. “Our goal is to be responsive and easy to work with, so our partners can move quickly, feel confident in referring opportunities, and deliver the best outcomes for their clients.”

That commitment is reflected in DUCA’s Business Loan solutions. Businesses can apply online in just minutes for unsecured business loans and lines of credit from $5,000 to $250,000, providing a simple and convenient way to access the capital needed to support growth initiatives, working capital requirements, expansion plans, and day-to-day operations. For financing needs exceeding $250,000, a DUCA Business Banking Advisor can be contacted directly to explore customized lending solutions. Combined with quick turnaround times and direct access to decision-makers, DUCA provides a reliable financing partner for businesses seeking flexible access to capital.

For PFG Financial, the value comes from having a partner that combines speed with accessibility. “Working with DUCA feels like an extension of our own team,” says LaMar VanDusen, Managing Director at PFG Financial. “We get fast answers, real collaboration, and a partner who understands what we’re trying to achieve. That makes it easier for us to deliver for our clients.”

As a member-focused financial institution, DUCA works closely with business consultants, accountants, and centres of influence to help businesses access the financing they need to achieve their goals. For firms like PFG Financial, direct access to decision-makers and flexible lending solutions help make that process simpler and more effective for the businesses they support.

“What we’re building is more than a referral channel, it’s a true partnership,” says Mo Mauri, Chief Commercial Banking Officer at DUCA. “When we make it easier for business consultants and accountants to do business with us through speed, clarity, and consistency, we’re helping them better serve their clients while supporting business growth across Ontario.”

Whether it’s an unsecured business loan, a business line of credit, or a customized financing solution, DUCA is committed to helping Ontario businesses access the capital they need to grow with confidence.

beyond-the-tariff-rate.title: Beyond the Tariff Rate: What Canadian Importers Need to Know as U.S.–Canada Trade Rules Shift
beyond-the-tariff-rate.author: Maheen Bari
beyond-the-tariff-rate.alt: Beyond the Tariff Rate — UPS trade webinar for Canadian importers
beyond-the-tariff-rate.excerpt: Section 338, Executive Order 14411 and landed-cost visibility: what cross-border SMEs should check now on classification, origin and compliance.
beyond-the-tariff-rate.html:
Canadian importers will face higher tariffs, customs restrictions, and compliance concerns. If you attended UPS’s trade webinar on September 10, you learned what businesses need to know. Tariffs are becoming a minor part of a much larger challenge for Canadian small and medium-sized firms engaged in cross-border commerce. Changes in customs processes, product classifications, rules of origin, importer responsibilities, and landed charges are making it harder for businesses to move goods between Canada and the United States.

UPS hosted a webinar titled Beyond the Tariff Rate: What US and Canadian Importers Need to Do Next on September 10, 2026, at 11:00 AM EST. The event covered recent Canada-U.S. trade developments and offered practical advice for firms considering costs, compliance duties, and cross-border operations.

Canada-U.S. Trade Is Entering Another Critical Period

The United States remains Canada’s top merchandise export market. In 2025, the United States received 71.7% of Canada’s merchandise exports, down from 75.9% in 2024. Canada’s product exports to the United States fell by 5.8 percent in 2025. Small enterprises are particularly vulnerable to changes south of the border.

According to Innovation, Science, and Economic Development Canada, SMEs accounted for 73.3% of Canadian firms exporting goods in 2024 and 37.9% of the total value of Canadian goods exports. In 2024, the United States received 79.4 percent of small firms’ export value.

Because of this concentration, changes in tariffs, customs processes, or importer obligations can significantly affect Canadian companies’ margins, pricing, and supply chain considerations.

Why Section 338 Matters to Canadian Businesses

Section 338 of the United States Tariff Act of 1930 is a key topic covered in the webinar. Section 338 authorizes the President of the United States to apply extra charges of up to 50% in response to what the administration deems discriminatory or unequal treatment of US commerce by another country. In July 2026, the US administration used Section 338 to impose additional 50% tariffs on certain Canadian products, including dairy, alcoholic beverages, and motor vehicles. Following a temporary hiatus, the extra obligations took effect on August 22.

Canada subsequently announced countermeasures. Effective September 8, 2026, Canada imposed tariffs of 15%, 25%, and 50% on $27.6 billion in U.S. imports, focusing on steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper, plastics, and electronics. These measures make it even more vital for SMEs to understand precise tariff classification, place of origin, and total landed cost.

Executive Order 14411 Raises the Compliance Bar

Importers must watch more than just tariff rates. On June 3, 2026, the United States released Executive Order 14411, Strengthening Customs Enforcement, which advocates for increased customs enforcement and greater accountability for registered importers. The order focuses on importer identification, duty collection, forced labour restrictions, country of origin, origin marking, intellectual property, and product safety.

The order also instructs the US Department of Homeland Security to update regulations, guidance, and procedures related to importer eligibility within 180 days. For enterprises shipping into the United States, this guidance emphasizes the significance of precise documentation and internal trade compliance procedures.

Companies may need to investigate beyond the simple question, “What tariff applies?” Instead, they should ask:

  • Is the product classified using the correct Harmonized System code?
  • Does the declared country of origin have the necessary documentation to support it?
  • Who is the importer of record?
  • Are the customs values calculated correctly?
  • Is the shipment eligible for applicable preferential treatment or tariff relief?
  • What is the true landed cost after taking into account tariffs, levies, taxes, and other expenses?

Landed Cost Visibility Becomes a Business Strategy

For SMEs with thin margins, an unexpected customs fee can transform a profitable shipment into an unprofitable one. This is why landed cost visibility is evolving beyond a logistics function. It is progressively influencing price strategy, supplier selection, procurement decisions, and customer experience. Canadian businesses should model various tariff situations before goods reach the border, rather than assessing their risk after customs clearance.

The Canadian government also maintains tariff remission methods in specific cases. Businesses that can’t get necessary inputs locally or fairly from non-US suppliers may be eligible to request exceptional tariff relief, depending on their eligibility and the items involved.

What the UPS Webinar Covered

UPS-organised September 10th session focused on five key areas: Section 338 and its two-way influence on Canada-United States commerce; Executive Order 14411 and changing importer expectations; current customs and trade rules; compliance risk management techniques; and options for classification reviews, customs support, and increased landed cost visibility.

The webinar featured UPS experts in trade policy, customs, public affairs, and cross-border commerce, including Catherine Mellor, Vice President of Global Public Affairs; Jessica Rosen, Senior Director of UPS Trade Advisory Services; Carolyn Kim, Vice President of Public Affairs for UPS Canada; Brian Huh, Product Manager; and Penny Moulton, Director of Trade Management Services and Trade Compliance. Together, these perspectives are anticipated to link policy changes with practical actions. Their insights are expected to connect legislative advances with the practical considerations firms must make when shipping items across borders.

What Canadian SMEs Should Do Now

Canadian firms do not need to wait for another tariff notification before assessing their exposure. Importers and exporters can start by analyzing product categories, confirming origin documents, reviewing supplier and customer contracts, modelling landed costs under various tariff scenarios, and identifying areas where their supply chains still rely heavily on a single marketplace.

For organizations without dedicated internal customs or foreign trade teams, specialist advice can also help uncover gaps before they become costly compliance issues. Preparedness is becoming increasingly crucial as Canada’s and the United States’ trade policies accelerate. Businesses that understand their risk, have accurate data, and can swiftly forecast the financial impact of a regulation change will be better prepared to respond.

This webinar was for firms seeking to better understand tariff risk, customs compliance, and the practical ramifications of recent Canada-United States trade developments.

business-woman-of-the-month-nouhaila-che.html:
Scaling Opportunity for Immigrant Tech Talent in Canada with Nouhaila Chelkhaoui

Nouhaila Chelkhaoui, who came to Canada alone at the age of 17, soon learned that even a top-notch degree does not guarantee access to opportunities, particularly if you are a newcomer, a person of colour, and pursuing a profession far from home. Her life’s work was fueled by that encounter. As the founder and CEO of Scale Without Borders, she now oversees what has grown into Canada’s largest network for immigrant tech talent, connecting thousands of immigrants with the businesses, funding, and community they need to succeed. 

From Newcomer Struggle to Systems‑Level Solution 

Like many immigration journeys, Nouhaila’s narrative begins with a different response. After arriving in Canada as a teenager, she had to adjust to a new language and culture before graduating from one of the world’s best universities, the University of Toronto. Nevertheless, she found it “extremely difficult” to enter the workforce as an immigrant despite having that qualification. 

All around her, she observed the same pattern: exceptionally talented immigrants with stellar records in engineering, product, data, and leadership positions overseas were abruptly forced into survival jobs or never-ending application cycles. Systemic obstacles, such as recruiting procedures that favour “Canadian experience,” a lack of networks, and credential bias, were the problem rather than a lack of talent. 

Instead of just persevering on her own, Nouhaila chose to create a system that would make things simpler, more transparent, and fairer for those who would follow in her footsteps. That system is Scale Without Borders, which is based on firsthand knowledge and a thorough comprehension of both immigration and technology.

Building Scale Without Borders

For Canadian immigrant IT talent, Scale Without Borders (SWB) serves as a community, platform, and catalyst. Under Nouhaila’s direction, it has expanded into the nation’s largest network dedicated to tech novices, helping over 6,000 individuals through contacts, events, and programs.

SWB offers the following to immigrant tech professionals: 

  • EMPLOYER CONNECTIONS: Private career fairs with employers; get face time with recruiters actively hiring
  • EXCLUSIVE EVENTS: In-person events like networking events, social nights, brunches, coffee meetups, walks, and runs + access to passes for conferences, including Elevate Festival, Collision, Web Summit, Toronto Tech Week and more
  • COMMUNITY & NETWORKS: An online community and WhatsApp group to connect, share opportunities, and stay supported. Gain exclusive free/discounted access to top tech events, curated referrals, and warm introductions (e.g., trusted immigration lawyers, founder communities, or connections within our VC and investor networks).
  • HANDS-ON LEARNING: Monthly hands-on workshops with guest speakers and experts designed to give you a real edge in your career + Access to hundreds of hours of self-paced tech training across cybersecurity, AI, coding, and more in over 10 languages.
  • FLAGSHIP SUMMIT: Access to the annual Immigrants Tech Summit at ROM.

The organization also offers a 30-day free trial, during which folks can cancel anytime via the portal.

SWB serves as a bridge for companies, including big banks, fast-growing tech scaleups, government, and non-profits, to access vetted, high-calibre talent outside typical recruiting approaches. These collaborations have enabled businesses to fill crucial tasks while also establishing more diverse, globally thinking teams. 

The organization has been featured in publications such as the Toronto Star, the Globe and Mail, Bay Street Bull, and Betakit, and has received accolades including a “Top 100 Companies to Watch” designation and a Women of Influence award. These accolades demonstrate that immigrant-led, impact-driven enterprises can compete with typical high-growth ventures. 

A Career of Championing Founders and Newcomers 

Scale Without Borders is not Nouhaila’s first experience developing ecosystems. She formerly oversaw Women Founders programs at the DMZ, a leading startup incubator in Canada, before pursuing SWB full-time. She assisted hundreds of early-stage and scaling firms, including those led by women and other underrepresented founders, in raising capital, acquiring strategic clients, and building their teams. 

Her role provided insight into the impact of support systems on a founder’s success, including access to investors, mentorship, and peer communities, which can reduce years of trial and error to months. She applied the same principle to SWB, building it not as a job board, but as an ecosystem in which mentorship, community, and opportunity interact. 

Previously, Nouhaila managed an initiative to help Syrian refugees navigate Canada’s convoluted healthcare system, which was reported by TechCrunch, HuffPost, and Metro News. She also helped establish a health-tech firm. Those experiences honed her grasp of what it means to design for people who are rebuilding their lives despite administrative and cultural obstacles. She has lived and worked in Brazil, Turkey, and Morocco, and speaks English, Arabic (Moroccan), French, and conversational Spanish. She offers a truly global perspective to her work in Canadian technology. 

Redefining What “Tech Talent” Looks Like

Narrative transformation is a common theme in Nouhaila’s works. She questions the notion that “tech talent” must appear or sound a certain way—or come from a specific set of institutions and companies. She emphasizes the importance of global perspectives, multilingual communication, and cross-market experience by focusing on immigrant founders and professionals. 

SWB’s events and storytelling platforms showcase engineers who built products for millions of users worldwide, product managers who navigated hypergrowth in emerging markets, and founders who bootstrapped companies under conditions more challenging than those faced by most Canadian startups. In doing so, she reframes newcomers as a competitive advantage for Canadian innovation, rather than a charity case. 

Lessons for CanadianSME Readers

Nouhaila’s story teaches clear lessons to small business owners and founders: 

  • Design from personal experience: she based SWB on the pain spots she encountered—and noticed around her. 
  • Think ecosystem, not just enterprise: by servicing both talent and employers, SWB increases its influence. 
  • Lead with both credibility and vulnerability: she is upfront about her own struggles, making her a true, trustworthy leader for those who follow her. 

Conclusion

From coming alone to Canada at the age of 17 to running a national platform for immigrant tech talent, Nouhaila Chelkhaoui has transformed personal hurdles into a roadmap for systemic change. Her work at Scale Without Borders exemplifies the founder-driven, impact-oriented leadership that CanadianSME is proud to highlight.

why-human-communication-matters-more-in-.html:
In this exclusive CanadianSME Small Business Magazine interview, Steve Brennan, Co-Founder & General Manager of Stand Up and Speak Inc., shares insights from his entrepreneurial journey in communication education, leadership, recruitment, and executive search. Since 2001, Steve has helped grow Stand Up and Speak from just four students in a basement into a trusted communication academy serving individuals, families, schools, and businesses.

Steve is also the Founder & CEO of Top Quality Recruitment (TQR), a national recruitment and executive-search firm serving organizations across North America. Through both companies, Steve is passionate about connecting people with opportunity—helping individuals communicate with confidence while helping businesses find the exceptional talent and leaders they need to succeed.

After 25 years of teaching public speaking, what has remained most important about building confidence?

Confidence is built through action. That has not changed in 25 years.

Many people assume someone must first feel confident before speaking. In reality, confidence usually comes afterward. A student stands up, speaks despite feeling nervous, receives constructive feedback, and tries again. Each successful attempt provides evidence that they can handle the challenge.

The goal is not to eliminate nervousness. Even experienced speakers get nervous. The goal is to help people manage those feelings so they can communicate effectively anyway.

We also have to recognize that every student begins in a different place. For one student, success may mean delivering a polished speech. For another, it may mean making eye contact, answering a question in a complete sentence, or speaking loudly enough to be heard. Those small improvements can be enormous victories.

Confidence grows when people move beyond their comfort zones in a supportive environment. You cannot simply tell someone to be confident. You have to give them opportunities to take a leap outside of their comfort zone, practice, improve, and discover that making a mistake is not a disaster.

Why are human skills like listening, clear thinking, and answering unscripted questions becoming more valuable in the AI era?

Human communication skills are more valuable than ever in the age of AI

AI can help people research, organize ideas, and prepare stronger written material. What it cannot do is replace the human being when the conversation moves away from the script.

In business, interviews, classrooms, and leadership situations, people must listen carefully, understand what is actually being asked, and respond thoughtfully in the moment. A polished presentation means very little if the speaker cannot answer a reasonable follow-up question.

There is also a risk that people will become too dependent on AI-generated language. The words may sound impressive, but if the person cannot explain or defend them, credibility disappears quickly.

As AI makes information and prepared content easier to produce, distinctly human abilities become even more valuable. These include judgment, curiosity, empathy, clear thinking, and the ability to build trust through conversation.

AI should help us communicate more effectively, but it should not do all our thinking for us. Future leaders will need to use technology intelligently while still being able to look someone in the eye, ask a thoughtful question, listen to the answer, and respond without needing a machine to whisper the next line or tell them what to say or think.

How has technology—from social media to AI—changed the communication challenges faced by children and adults?

Technology has given people more ways to communicate, but more communication does not necessarily mean better communication.

Children can become comfortable texting, posting, or interacting through a screen while still struggling to speak in front of a group, join a conversation, or answer an unexpected question. Adults face a similar problem. Email, messaging platforms, and virtual meetings allow us to avoid many uncomfortable conversations, but avoiding them does not improve our ability to handle them.  Handling difficult conversation will always be a part of life, particularly, in our professions, in business and interactions.  Technology is not going to change that, and we shouldn’t expect AI to do the heavy lifting of replacing the moments that challenge us.

Social media has also increased the pressure to appear polished. People see edited videos and carefully prepared content and assume effective speakers never hesitate, forget a word, or make mistakes. That is simply not true.

AI adds another challenge because it can produce professional-looking answers almost instantly. The danger is that people may present ideas they have not fully considered or cannot explain in their own words.

Technology is not the enemy. We use technology to make learning more accessible and to connect with students beyond our physical classrooms. However, it should support real practice, coaching, feedback, and human interaction. It cannot replace them.

What lessons did you learn growing Stand Up and Speak from a small basement program into a broader communication academy?

The first lesson is that growth begins with solving a real problem well. 

Stand Up and Speak started with four or five students in a basement back in 2001, not with a grand expansion plan. We focused on helping those students become stronger and more confident communicators, one student at a time.

The second lesson is that reputation is built one experience at a time. Parents trust us with their children, and adults often come to us when communication is affecting their careers or confidence. That trust cannot be taken for granted and in spite of our growth, each student remains critical to our success, that’s why we keep our class sizes small and continue to offer one-on-one coaching for all ages.

We also learned that a good program cannot depend entirely on the personality or instincts of one instructor. To grow, we needed clear teaching methods, rigorous training, strong instructors, consistent expectations, and the ability to meet students at different skill levels.

Finally, you have to evolve without losing sight of what made the organization valuable. We have expanded into camps, competitive programs, private coaching, adult training, and live online learning across the globe. The delivery methods have changed, but the foundation has not.

After 25 years, our purpose remains straightforward: give people a supportive place to practice, challenge themselves, receive useful feedback, and become more capable communicators.

Through your work in both recruitment and communication training, what skills do you believe future leaders need most? 

Future leaders will need judgment, adaptability, accountability, and the ability to communicate clearly when the answer is not obvious.

Through recruitment, I see organizations place considerable value on technical experience. That experience matters, but leadership problems are rarely caused by a lack of technical vocabulary. They are more often caused by unclear expectations, poor listening, avoided conversations, weak decisions, and an inability to earn trust.  This is particularly stark when technical leaders are in management or supervisor roles, it doesn’t matter how strong they are technically, it matters how well they are able to communicate and lead their teams to higher performance.

Strong leaders must be able to explain what needs to happen and why. They must ask thoughtful questions, listen to people who disagree with them, and respond without becoming defensive. They also need the courage to make decisions with incomplete information and take responsibility for the outcome.

AI will give future leaders access to more information and faster analysis. It will not relieve them of responsibility for judgment. In fact, it may make judgment more important because leaders will need to separate useful insight from confident-sounding nonsense.

The best leaders will combine technological ability with human credibility. People still want to know that their leader understands the issue, can communicate honestly, empathize when required, and will remain steady when the script stops working.

Expansion to trade-management software timed to support businesses managing supply chain risk

Livingston International, a leading provider of trade management, trade consulting, customs brokerage and freight forwarding services has announced a timely expansion to its highly successful TradeSphere software that now includes Classifier and Free Trade Manager, allowing importers to effectively manage core trade processes and data within one application.

The longstanding technology has been helping business for more than 30 years manage their trade activity, and is now being expanded at precisely the time businesses need it the most.

“Over the past 18 months, we have seen unprecedented complexity introduced into trade processes and equally unprecedented scrutiny of customs entries and associated documentation,” said Livingston Chief Executive, Robert Smith. “In response, global businesses need tech solutions that combine the knowledge of trade experts with an easy-to-use interface they can access any time to simplify core aspects of customs processes.”

New to TradeSphere are capabilities that allow international businesses engaged in trade to:

  • Gain critical, automated product-classification management support.
  • Establish seamless processes for soliciting suppliers for product information integral to duty avoidance.
  • Have a simplified means of qualifying goods under free trade agreements.

Each of these can be performed within a single workflow. Data and documents are fed into consolidated reports, providing ease of access and quick reference in a manner that is aligned with audit requirements should businesses be called upon by customs officials to verify data.

“By harnessing the potential of Large Language Models (LLM) we’re making Livingston’s deep trade expertise more accessible, automated and scalable for international businesses,” said Karen Jasper, vice-president, Product Management and Marketing, Livingston International. “At a time when regulatory change is happening quickly and often with little notice, importers and exporters need affordable ways to reduce compliance risk, ease manual effort and identify cost-saving opportunities. That’s exactly what TradeSphere is designed to deliver.”

TradeSphere is an ideal solution for global enterprises that have the internal resources and expertise to take the reins of their trade and compliance programs using a software that offers centralized workflows and data ownership. It’s a scalable solution for companies with expanding product lists and/or international trade requirements, offering full audit trails and visibility.

“We continue to be a people-serving-people business,” said Smith. “As we continue our adoption and advancement of emerging technologies, we remain acutely aware that the expertise and experiences of our associates are what distinguish us, and that the needs and challenges of the people we service will always remain our north star. Our technologies are there to connect our clients with our trade intelligence so that they can better manage their global supply chains.”

For more information about Livingston’s expanded TradeSphere, please visit Livingston’s Global Trade Management page.

To request a demo, please fill out the form on our TradeSphere page.

Livingston International has served as a trusted trade adviser to businesses around the world for 80 years. It specializes in customs brokerage and trade compliance, and offers international trade consulting, global trade management and freight forwarding. Livingston provides clarity in a world of trade complexity, and reliability in times of volatility, so businesses can grow further, smarter and with confidence. Livingston employs approximately 2,700 associates at key border points, sea ports, airports and other strategic locations across North America, Europe and Asia. canadian-sponsorship-landscape-study-mar.html:
The Canadian Sponsorship Landscape Study (CSLS), Canada’s longest-running and only national-level benchmark of the sponsorship industry, is marking its 20th anniversary. The 2026 edition, released today by T1 and its partners IMI International (IMI), Sponsorship Marketing Council Canada (SMCC) and SponsorshipX, finds sponsorship spending in Canada has grown to $4.7 billion, with brands committing more to rights fees in a stable and balanced way across categories. Brands and properties reported planning to spend more next year.

Professional sport remains home to the largest and most impactful sponsorships, but brands are expanding into more categories. Cause is now the second-largest category by proportion of budgets and the third-largest for total sponsor spending, a drastic shift over the past decade. The 2026 FIFA World Cup also mattered to Canadian brands this year, with numerous activations planned around the tournament, reinforcing the pull of global mega-events.

The findings also point to real pressure points. Sponsorship’s share of the marketing communications budget at Canadian brands has slipped from 25 per cent to 21 per cent over the past five years, even as total spend climbs. Property servicing of brand partners took a step backward this year, with brands reporting unmet expectations. ROI remains the top issue for brands, properties and agencies, with the focus increasingly on maximizing value and demonstrating effectiveness.

“Twenty years ago, there was no Canadian-specific data for this industry to plan against. Today, the CSLS provides the numbers that brands, properties and agencies use to benchmark their decisions,” said Dr. Norm O’Reilly, partner at T1 and lead author of the CSLS, and professor and director of The Sponsorship Lab at the University of Florida. “This year’s findings show an industry that keeps maturing, from record investment in evaluation to how quickly brands moved on FIFA 2026.”

Looking ahead, sponsors and properties are bullish on 2026, forecasting a 12 per cent increase in spend, though agencies are more cautious about future billings. Evaluation has become a bigger investment priority than ever, with brands spending more on evaluation and pre-sponsorship evaluation than the CSLS has recorded in 20 years of tracking the market, a sign that brands are being asked to prove sponsorship works, not just fund it.

“Twenty years of data confirms what we see every day: sponsorship succeeds when it earns a real place in people’s lives, not just visibility on a logo board,” said Lindsay O’Brien, vice president, partnerships, T1 and co-author of the CSLS. “This year’s findings on evaluation and servicing tell us brands and properties are being held to that higher bar, and the ones investing in real relationships with their communities, not just rights fees, are the ones getting rewarded.”

The 20th annual CSLS draws on responses from 188 Canadian brands, properties and agencies (114 brands, 50 properties and 24 agencies), continuing two decades of tracking the size and scope of the market, spending by sector, activation trends, evaluation practices and where the industry is headed next. The study is produced by lead author Dr. Norm O’Reilly with co-authors Lindsay O’Brien and Mike Alcorn, alongside partners the SMCC, IMI, SponsorshipX and the Association of Canadian Advertisers. The full report is available here.

About the Canadian Sponsorship Landscape Study

The Canadian Sponsorship Landscape Study (CSLS) is Canada’s longest-running barometer on the sponsorship industry and the only national-level study of its kind. Now in its 20th year, the study launched after delegates at the inaugural Canadian Sponsorship Forum in Vancouver flagged a gap the industry could not ignore: no Canadian-specific data to plan against. Anderson College and Columbia Southern University (CSU) have entered into a new articulation and pathway agreement that expands educational opportunities for Anderson graduates by creating streamlined pathways into Columbia Southern University’s online bachelor’s and graduate degree programs.

The agreement establishes a collaborative framework that recognizes prior learning, facilitates transfer credit, and provides eligible Anderson graduates, employees, and their immediate families with access to Columbia Southern University’s Learning Partner benefits, including a 10 percent tuition discount. Together, the two institutions are creating flexible opportunities for lifelong learning while helping graduates grow professionally through higher education.

The pathway initially includes transfer credit opportunities for graduates of Anderson College’s Cardiology Technology, Diagnostic Medical Sonography, Medical Laboratory Technology-Hybrid, Occupational Health and Safety and Intra Oral Level I & II Dental Assistant programs. Coursework within these programs will be evaluated toward a variety of Columbia Southern University undergraduate degree programs, including the Bachelor of Science in Healthcare Administration, Bachelor of Science in Emergency Medical Services Administration, and Bachelor of Science in Business Administration. Additional Anderson College programs may be evaluated for transfer opportunities as the partnership continues to grow.

“Strong academic partnerships create opportunities for students to move forward with confidence and purpose,” said Janell Gibson, Ph.D., Provost and Chief Academic Officer of Columbia Southern University. “Our collaboration with Anderson College of Health, Business & Technology strengthens the pathway between institutions, helping students build upon their education, pursue their professional goals, and achieve continued academic success.”

“Our job is to help students succeed–not just while they’re at Anderson, but long after they graduate,” said Rose Elia, Chief Operating Officer of Anderson College. “This partnership gives our graduates another opportunity to continue learning whenever the time is right for them. It’s about making sure they have choices and know we’ll continue cheering them on as they grow in their careers.”

“This agreement is meaningful because it recognizes the learning our students have already completed,” said Cheryl Russell-Julien, Director of Academics and Quality Assurance at Anderson College. “Students should not have to start from the beginning when they have already built strong knowledge and skills. This pathway helps them take the next step with confidence, while still protecting the quality and expectations of the credential they are working toward.”

“For me, this partnership is about creating more possibilities for our students,” said Heather Yang, President and Chief Executive Officer of Anderson College. “So many students come to Anderson because they want a better career and a better life for themselves and their families. Graduation is an important milestone, but it doesn’t have to be the end of their learning. Through this pathway with Columbia Southern University, our graduates will have another opportunity to continue their education, open new doors, and build the careers they have been working so hard toward.”

Through the agreement, prospective students will have access to a dedicated Columbia Southern University partner portal outlining transfer opportunities and degree options. Eligible participants will also benefit from CSU’s flexible online learning model, complimentary evaluations of prior education and training, digital textbooks provided at no additional cost, and multiple course scheduling options designed to accommodate working professionals.

For more information about Anderson College and its programs, visit www.andersoncollege.com.

For more information about Columbia Southern University, visit www.columbiasouthern.edu.

About Columbia Southern University

Columbia Southern University is an accredited online university based in Orange Beach, Alabama, offering associate, bachelor’s, master’s, and doctoral degree programs across a wide range of disciplines. Through flexible online delivery and a commitment to serving working professionals, CSU provides accessible educational opportunities designed to support lifelong learning.

About Anderson College

Anderson College is one of Canada’s oldest colleges, having opened its first location in 1885. Anderson has trained more than 150,000 students over its 140-plus-year history and continues to be an empowering partner for students overcoming career challenges and transitioning to the next phase of their lives. With ten locations across Ontario, it is recognized for its high-calibre faculty, hands-on, real-life career training, and supportive culture.

Ten Two Partners today announced its official launch, introducing a new founder-focused venture accelerator designed to help promising Canadian entrepreneurs transform ambitious ideas into structured, investable and scalable businesses.

Founded by entrepreneur Reuben Ross, who brings more than three decades of operating experience and multiple successful business exits, Ten Two Partners was created to address one of the most difficult challenges facing early-stage founders: gaining access to the experience, resources and professional network required to turn a promising idea into a real company.

“There are incredible entrepreneurs across Canada with potentially game-changing ideas, but an idea alone isn’t enough,” said Ross, Founder & CEO of Ten Two Partners. “Too many founders are forced to learn every lesson the hard way. Our goal is to put experienced people, proven resources and the right relationships around them much earlier in the journey.”

Unlike traditional incubators or consulting firms, Ten Two Partners works alongside founders, providing hands-on strategic and execution support across the disciplines that can determine whether an early-stage company succeeds or fails.

  • Business strategy and company formation
  • Corporate and legal structuring
  • Financial architecture and accounting
  • Non-dilutive government funding and grants
  • Product and technology development
  • Branding, positioning and early traction
  • Capital readiness and fundraising preparation
  • Strategic and executive advisory

The Ten Two model is built around a simple principle: founders need more than advice – they need experienced people willing to help them build.

The firm works with a select group of early-stage entrepreneurs, including first-time founders and pre-revenue startups, helping them establish the legal, financial, operational and strategic foundations necessary to attract capital and scale successfully.

“We don’t want to stand on the sidelines telling founders what they should do,” Ross said. “We want to be in their corner helping them do it – making better decisions, avoiding expensive mistakes and building the fundamentals that sophisticated investors expect to see.”

Control Before Speed

The Ten Two name reflects the firm’s philosophy. Just as keeping your hands at ten and two represents control and readiness before accelerating, Ten Two Partners believes sustainable growth begins with getting the fundamentals right.

Control before speed. Structure before scale.

That philosophy is increasingly relevant in a startup environment where founders are being asked to demonstrate stronger business fundamentals, greater capital efficiency and clearer paths to sustainable growth.

Rather than focusing solely on fundraising, Ten Two Partners helps founders build companies that are ready for capital before pursuing it – with stronger structures, better financial visibility, clearer positioning and a more credible investment proposition.

“Raising money shouldn’t be the starting point,” Ross added. “Building something worth investing in should be. If we do that properly, capital becomes part of the growth strategy rather than the entire strategy.”

before-you-add-more-ai-strengthen-the-bu.html:
AI becomes far more valuable when it understands the business it is being asked to support.

Across Canada, small businesses are being encouraged to adopt artificial intelligence at a remarkable pace.

AI can help draft emails, create content, summarize meetings, analyze information, support customer service and reduce repetitive administrative work. For founders managing multiple responsibilities, that potential is understandably appealing.

But before adding another AI tool, there is a more important question to ask:

Is the business behind the AI clear enough for the technology to support it well?

AI does not automatically understand how a business operates. It does not know which clients are the right fit, how a founder makes decisions, what the brand should sound like, where human judgment is essential or what a great client experience looks like.

It can only work with the context it has been given.

When that context is missing, the problem is often blamed on the technology. The AI sounds generic. Its recommendations feel disconnected from the business. Drafts require extensive editing. Team members receive different answers, and the founder spends more time correcting the output than benefiting from it.

The business may not need better prompts. It may need a stronger foundation.

AI exposes what has not yet been made clear

Many small businesses carry essential knowledge inside the founder’s head.

The founder knows which clients are a good match, how an inquiry should be handled and what needs to happen before work begins. They can recognize when an email sounds wrong, even if the company’s voice has never been formally defined. They understand the exceptions, preferences and unwritten standards that keep the business running.

This approach can work when the founder is personally involved in almost every decision. It becomes much harder to maintain as the business adds employees, contractors, systems or AI tools.

AI tends to expose these gaps quickly.

If a business has not clearly defined its process, AI may accelerate an inconsistent one. If important knowledge is scattered across inboxes, documents and individual team members, AI cannot reliably determine which information should guide its response. If the company’s communication standards exist only through instinct, AI will fill in the blanks with generic language.

That is why AI readiness is not simply a technology question. It is also a business infrastructure question.

Start with the work, not the tool

Before selecting an AI solution, founders should identify the business outcome they are trying to improve.

Is the goal to respond to inquiries more consistently? Reduce the time spent drafting routine communication? Improve onboarding? Organize internal knowledge? Help a team follow the same process?

Once the desired outcome is clear, the business can examine the workflow behind it.

For example, before using AI to support client onboarding, a company should be able to explain:

  1. What triggers the onboarding process?
  2. What information must be collected?
  3. Who is responsible for each step?
  4. What should the client receive and when?
  5. Which decisions require human approval?
  6. What does a successful onboarding experience look like?

If those answers are unclear, introducing AI may create speed without creating consistency.

A clear process gives the technology something dependable to support.

Give AI a business brain

AI performs better when it has access to organized, approved business context. This might include the company’s positioning, ideal client profile, services, decision rules, workflows, communication standards and examples of high quality work.

Together, this information acts like a business brain.

It helps AI understand not only what the company does, but how the company thinks and communicates.

This does not require a large corporate knowledge system. A small business can begin by documenting a few foundational areas:

Business clarity: What does the company do, who does it serve and what problems does it solve?

Workflow structure: How does important work move from one stage to the next?

Knowledge infrastructure: Where is the information required to complete that work stored?

Communication standards: How should the business sound in different situations?

Human review boundaries: Which outputs can assist the team, and which decisions must remain with a person?

These foundations make it easier to use AI consistently across different tools and team members.

They also remain valuable if the business changes platforms later.

Keep human judgment visible

Stronger AI does not reduce the importance of human leadership. It makes clear human leadership even more necessary.

A business should decide where AI can draft, organize, suggest or summarize, as well as where a person must review, approve or make the final decision.

Routine internal summaries may require only a quick accuracy check. Client communication involving conflict, pricing, commitments or sensitive information may need careful review. Strategic decisions should remain grounded in the founder’s experience, values and understanding of the business.

The goal is not to remove people from the work. It is to use AI where it can provide practical support while protecting the judgment, relationships and accountability that belong to humans.

Build clarity before complexity

Small businesses do not need to adopt every new AI tool to remain competitive. They need to understand where AI can create meaningful value and whether the business is prepared to support that use.

Before adding more technology, take one important workflow and document how it should operate. Gather the knowledge required to support it. Define the communication standards and identify the points where human review is necessary.

Then introduce AI with a clear purpose.

The businesses that gain the greatest value from AI may not be the ones using the most tools. They may be the ones that have taken the time to strengthen the knowledge, processes and judgment behind them.

Many businesses are using AI.

Far fewer are preparing the business behind it.

That preparation is where better results begin.

About Author

Jennifer Smart is the founder of Luxe AI Concierge, a Canadian human-led AI and businessinfrastructure consultancy. She helps founders organize the knowledge, workflows and communication standards behind their businesses so they can work with AI more clearly, consistently and confidently.

AI is changing the way businesses work. From improving customer experiences and analyzing information to streamlining workflows and supporting better decisions, organizations are finding new ways to bring AI into their day-to-day operations.

But for many small and medium-sized businesses, the challenge is not understanding that AI matters. The challenge is figuring out where to start.

Many business leaders are asking the same practical questions: Where can AI create real value for our business? Which processes are worth exploring? How do we experiment without creating unnecessary risk? And how do we make progress when our teams are already balancing competing priorities?

These questions do not mean businesses are falling behind. They show that employers want to approach AI in a way that makes sense for their teams, customers, and operations.

The reality is that AI adoption is moving quickly, but confidence in using AI effectively has not kept pace. McKinsey’s 2025 Global AI Survey found that 88% of organizations regularly use AI across at least one business function, yet many companies are still working to move beyond experimentation and achieve meaningful business impact.

For SMEs, that transition can feel even more challenging. Without large technology teams or dedicated AI specialists, deciding where to focus time, resources, and attention is not always straightforward.

The first step is not having every answer. It is finding the right place to begin.

Moving from AI interest to AI action

Most businesses understand that AI will play an important role in the future of work. The challenge is turning that awareness into practical action.

Riipen’s State of the employer highlights this gap. While 76.2% of employers say AI skills are a priority, 42.4% had not yet considered student projects as part of their AI strategy.

This is what Riipen refers to as the AI Action Gap: the space between knowing AI matters and having a clear, practical way to begin.

For many SMEs, closing this gap does not start with a large technology transformation or a complex AI implementation. It starts with identifying one meaningful opportunity.

  • Where could AI help reduce repetitive work?
  • Where could it improve an existing process?
  • Where could a business test an idea, learn from the results, and decide what to do next?

A first AI project does not need to transform an entire organization. Often, the most valuable first step is a focused experiment that helps a business understand where AI can support its work, where human expertise remains essential, and what opportunities are worth exploring further.

AI adoption starts with confidence, not complexity

One of the biggest misconceptions about AI is that businesses need advanced technical expertise to begin exploring its potential. In reality, many successful AI journeys start with something much simpler: understanding the business challenge first and identifying where AI could provide support.

For an SME, that might mean exploring ways to better understand customer feedback, improve internal processes, streamline repetitive tasks, support marketing efforts, or uncover new opportunities within existing workflows. The goal is not to introduce AI everywhere or chase the latest technology. It is to identify where AI can create meaningful value for the business and help teams work more effectively.

Why starting small can lead to bigger progress

When businesses think about AI, they often picture advanced automation, custom software, or complex technology projects. But for many SMEs, the most valuable first step is much more practical: starting with a focused business challenge, testing an idea, and learning what works before making larger investments.

This is where student-supported projects can create meaningful value. Students bring emerging skills, curiosity, and familiarity with new technologies, while employers bring the business context, customer understanding, and industry expertise needed to identify where AI can make a difference. Together, they create an opportunity to explore AI through real work, build confidence, and better understand where technology can support the business while keeping human judgment at the centre.

The result is more than a project deliverable. It is a clearer understanding of where AI can create value, what opportunities are worth exploring next, and how businesses can move forward with confidence.

Building a human-led approach to AI

The businesses that benefit most from AI will not necessarily be the ones using the most advanced tools. They will be the ones who understand where technology can support their work and where human expertise, experience, and judgment remain essential.

A human-led approach to AI adoption starts with the business challenge, not the technology. It means identifying where AI could create value, setting clear boundaries around how tools and information are used, and keeping people involved throughout the process. AI can help teams explore ideas, improve workflows, and support decision-making, but human judgment remains critical in determining what works, what needs to change, and what should come next.

The most effective way to build confidence with AI is through experimentation. Each project provides new insights into where technology can help, where additional support is needed, and how businesses can continue moving forward.

AI is not about replacing the expertise already inside a business. It is about creating new ways for people, technology, and emerging talent to work together to solve problems and create meaningful progress.

Taking the first step toward AI progress

Every SME is at a different stage of its AI journey. Some businesses are just beginning to explore what AI could mean for their organization, while others have already started experimenting but are unsure how to turn those early efforts into meaningful progress.

The challenge is that there is no one-size-fits-all approach to AI adoption. The right starting point depends on your business, your goals, your processes, and the opportunities where AI can create the most value.

Taking the time to understand your current readiness can help you identify where AI makes sense for your organization, where your team may need additional support, and what types of projects can help you move from curiosity to action.

Artificial intelligence has evolved from a futuristic concept to a useful corporate tool. Small and medium-sized businesses throughout Canada are experimenting with artificial intelligence to increase productivity, automate operations, and better understand their consumers. However, the biggest challenge for many SMEs is no longer whether they should employ AI, but how to turn these investments into measurable economic benefits. 

The CanadianSME Small Business Summit 2026, held this October at the Metro Toronto Convention Centre, will bring together industry leaders, innovators, and entrepreneurs under the theme “Beyond AI: Building Intelligent, Resilient, and Human-Centered Canadian SMEs” to discuss the next stage of AI transformation: moving beyond adoption and making a real impact.

One of the key sessions, “From AI Adoption to Real ROI: Turning Technology into Measurable Growth,” will look at how SMEs can move beyond AI testing to develop strategies that deliver real results. 

Moving Beyond AI Experimentation 

Businesses have swiftly adopted AI-powered technologies for a variety of functions, including content development, customer support, data analysis, and automation. While new technologies present substantial prospects, many SMEs struggle to determine which solutions add true value. The difficulty is not just having access to AI tools; it is about understanding how they connect with business goals. 

To successfully adopt AI, firms must pose critical questions: 

  • What business challenge are we attempting to solve?
  • How will artificial intelligence (AI) increase productivity and consumer experience?
  • What measurable outcomes can we expect?
  • How can we incorporate AI into our existing workflows?

The panel will discuss why firms should shift from a tool-focused perspective to a strategy-driven approach in which technology supports certain goals. 

Turning AI Investments Into Business Results 

Every investment must help SMEs grow, improve efficiency, or become more competitive. When applied correctly, AI has the potential to add tremendous value. 

Businesses are increasingly embracing AI for: 

  • Reduce repetitive administrative tasks.
  • Improve operational efficiency.Improve customer engagement
  • Make quick, data-driven decisions.
  • Identify new market opportunities.
  • Using clever automation to support employees

However, attaining true ROI takes more than just adopting AI software. Companies must understand how technology fits into their operations and assess its impact using meaningful performance indicators. AI success is dependent on integrating innovation with measurable business benefits, whether it is cost reduction or revenue growth.

Avoiding the Challenge of “Tool Overload” 

With thousands of AI solutions on the market, many firms confront an additional challenge: selecting the correct tools. The rapid advancement of AI technology has resulted in a crowded market in which corporations can invest in various platforms without a defined strategy. This can result in high costs, unconnected systems, and limited results. 

The panel will discuss how SMEs can avoid “tool overload” by concentrating on: 

  • Choosing solutions depending on business needs.
  • Integrating AI into Existing Systems
  • Prioritizing scalability and long-term value
  • Ensuring that employees can efficiently use new technologies.

Rather than adopting every emerging tool, businesses can achieve more success by developing a targeted AI roadmap that aligns with their goals. 

Building Smarter Workflows With Human-Centered AI 

While AI may alter company operations, its greatest value is realized when technology collaborates with people. The future of AI-powered organizations is not about replacing human expertise, but about improving decision-making, creativity, and efficiency. 

Human-centred AI enables SMEs to combine the efficiency of automation with the strategic thinking, relationships, and creativity that underpin entrepreneurial activity. Businesses can improve internal operations and deliver superior customer experiences by equipping employees with better tools and information.

Learning From Real-World AI Success Stories 

The panel will include specialists who understand the practical aspects of AI application. Attendees will get a better grasp of how businesses can progress from AI curiosity to AI success by reviewing industry insights, frameworks, and case studies. 

Participants will discuss strategies for: 

  • Measuring AI Performance and ROI
  • Identifying High-impact AI Opportunities
  • Developing successful implementation plans
  • Creating competitive advantages with technology

The purpose is to provide SMEs with actionable knowledge that they can instantly utilize in their enterprises.

The Next Chapter of AI for Canadian SMEs 

AI adoption is just the beginning. Businesses that understand how to translate technology into meaningful outcomes will thrive in the next few years. The CanadianSME Small Business Summit 2026 will provide entrepreneurs and business leaders with the knowledge they need to navigate this next phase, in which AI is about more than simply innovation, but also growth, resilience, and long-term impact. 

As Canadian SMEs look to the future, the question is no longer whether they should use AI. The question is how they can strategically apply it to create smarter, stronger, and more human-centred enterprises.

In this exclusive CanadianSME Small Business Magazine interview, Shawn Bedard, President & Founder of JIG Technologies, shares insights from more than 25 years of helping organizations turn complex technology into practical business solutions. A University of Waterloo engineering graduate, Shawn founded JIG Technologies in 2001 after gaining experience with organizations including CIBC, Sun Life, and IBM.

Today, JIG Technologies helps small and mid-sized businesses, nonprofits, and healthcare organizations strengthen their IT strategy, cybersecurity, and technology infrastructure. A strong advocate for putting business objectives before technology, Shawn helps leaders make smarter decisions around IT and AI while also mentoring entrepreneurs through Entrepreneurs’ Organization Toronto.

How can a business owner tell if their IT provider is genuinely doing a good job—not just closing support tickets?

While responding to and resolving tickets is an important measure, a business owner should look beyond how quickly tickets are closed. The focus should be on whether IT is becoming more reliable, secure and aligned with the business over time.

A strong IT provider should be reducing recurring problems, identifying risks before they become incidents, maintaining accurate documentation, planning for aging systems, testing backups, and providing a clear technology roadmap. Support should feel increasingly proactive, not like an endless cycle of fixing the same issues.

Good providers should also understand where the organization is going and communicate clearly with leadership. Leaders should receive explanations of risks, priorities and upcoming investments in business language, with enough context to understand why something matters and what outcome is expected. Technology recommendations should connect to business goals, not exist in isolation.

A warning sign is when the relationship is almost entirely ticket-driven, recurring issues remain unresolved, surprises are common, or leadership has little visibility into risks and future needs.

Ultimately, good IT support should create confidence that someone is actively looking after the technology environment—not simply waiting for the next problem to occur.

When an IT provider gives a long list of recommendations, how should a business decide what is urgent and what can wait?

When an IT provider gives a long list of recommendations, good advice should already come with clear prioritization.

A strong provider should distinguish between immediate risks, items that should be planned and budgeted for, and improvements that would be beneficial but are not urgent. Recommendations should be tied to business impact, security risk, compliance requirements, system reliability, and the organization’s goals—not simply presented as a technical wish list.

The timing should also make sense. Some items may need attention immediately, while others belong in a 12-, 24-, or even 36-month roadmap. Costs, dependencies and trade-offs should be clear enough that leadership can make informed decisions.

A warning sign is when everything is presented as critical, recommendations continually appear without a broader plan, or the provider cannot clearly connect the investment to a business outcome or meaningful reduction in risk.

Ultimately, a good IT provider should help leadership turn technology needs into a practical, prioritized roadmap—not overwhelm them with a list of things to buy.

How can leaders know their backups will actually work when a cyberattack, system failure, or disaster happens?

The most important answer is simple: test them.

Seeing a dashboard that says “backup successful” does not prove that the organization can actually recover. A successful restore test does. Leaders should know when the last restore test was performed, what was restored, whether it was successful and how long recovery took.

It is also important to understand what is actually being backed up. Is it a complete system that can be restored, or only selected files and data? Business owners often assume everything important is protected when, in reality, critical systems or information may have been overlooked.

Backup resilience matters as well. An on-site copy can provide faster recovery, while at least one protected off-site copy should be isolated from the production environment so the same ransomware attack or disaster cannot affect both.

Finally, leaders should understand the backup frequency and be comfortable with how much data could be lost between backups.

The goal is not to understand every technical detail. It is to have evidence that the organization can recover within a timeframe—and with an acceptable amount of data loss—that the business can live with.

Cybersecurity can feel like a bottomless expense. What does “good enough” protection look like for a small or midsized business?

“Good enough” does not mean eliminating all risk. That is neither realistic nor affordable. It means reducing the most significant risks to a level the business understands and accepts.

For most small and midsized organizations, I would start with strong fundamentals: multifactor authentication, timely patching, endpoint protection, secure backups, limited administrative access, employee security awareness, email protection and a documented incident response plan.

From there, security investments should be based on the organization’s actual risk. A healthcare organization holding sensitive personal information may need significantly stronger controls than a small business with limited confidential data.

The important part is having a framework rather than continually buying the newest security product.

Leadership should be able to answer: What are our biggest risks? Which controls reduce them? What gaps remain? And have we consciously accepted those gaps?

Cybersecurity spending becomes much easier to manage when it is connected to risk and business impact rather than fear.

How can a business tell whether its IT provider is recommending something because it is genuinely needed rather than because the provider profits from selling it?

This is a fair question, and every IT provider should be able to explain the value of a recommendation in terms that make sense to the business.

To get past the technical jargon, ask questions such as: What problem does this solve? What risk does it reduce? What happens if we do nothing? Are there less expensive alternatives?

Providers should also be transparent about where financial incentives exist. It is reasonable for an IT company to earn a margin on the products and services it provides, but clients should understand how recommendations are being made.

One of the best indicators of a trusted advisor is a willingness to sometimes recommend a less expensive option—or even recommend doing nothing when an investment is not yet necessary.

Trust develops when recommendations consistently reflect the client’s needs, budget and objectives rather than maximizing technology spend. If a provider cannot clearly explain why something is needed and how it provides value to the business, leadership should feel comfortable challenging the recommendation.

How can a nontechnical business leader effectively oversee IT without becoming an IT expert?

You do not need to become an IT expert any more than a business owner needs to become an accountant to oversee finance.

The starting point is being clear about the business strategy and communicating it to your IT provider. Leaders should be asking questions such as: Where are we trying to grow? What processes are holding us back? Where do we need greater efficiency? What risks could significantly disrupt the business? And what capabilities will our people need over the next few years?

From there, the technology questions become much easier: How is technology supporting those objectives? What are our biggest technology risks? What investments will we need over the next 12 to 24 months?

I also recommend maintaining a simple technology roadmap showing major risks, upcoming projects, expected costs and priorities.

A good IT advisor should translate technology into business impact. If overseeing IT requires you to understand every technical detail yourself, the relationship is not working properly.

If a business is unhappy with its IT provider, what should it know before deciding to switch?

Usually, the first step before switching is to be clear with the current provider about what is not working. It may be a misunderstanding around expectations or service needs. However, if it is clear the provider is no longer a good fit, changing IT providers should not be frightening when properly managed.

Start by reviewing the existing contract and understanding the termination terms. Also determine who owns and controls critical technology assets such as domains, Microsoft 365 accounts, administrative credentials, software licences, network equipment, backups, internet services, cloud systems and documentation. These should ultimately remain under the organization’s control.

The incoming provider should create a transition plan that covers documentation and credentials, security, backups, systems, immediate risks and knowledge transfer.

Where possible, avoid cancelling the existing provider too early and allow a short overlap between providers.

Most importantly, do not remain in a poor relationship simply because switching feels risky. A well-managed transition is less risky than continuing with a provider you no longer trust.

Good providers should make both onboarding and offboarding professional and orderly.

what-women-entrepreneurs-should-know-abo.title: What Women Entrepreneurs Should Know About Scam Investors
what-women-entrepreneurs-should-know-abo.author: CanadianSME
what-women-entrepreneurs-should-know-abo.alt: A woman wearing glasses and a beige blazer works on a laptop at a white desk in a modern office. A small green plant is in the foreground.

what-women-entrepreneurs-should-know-abo.html:
In Canada, one of the largest obstacles for female entrepreneurs is still access to funding. Compared with the norm for all enterprises, more than half of female entrepreneurs report difficulty obtaining financing, and their applications are denied more frequently. However, a lot of female entrepreneurs describe psychological obstacles related to debt and investments, such as concerns about losing control and being exploited by more experienced financial actors. 

Predatory lenders, phony “grant” providers, and scam investors may find the ideal opportunity to take advantage of the combination of genuine structural hurdles and reasonable caution. In order to develop confidently in 2026, female entrepreneurs will need both bravery and a playbook: useful tools to identify bad actors early, decline detrimental offers, and still boldly pursue the correct finance. 

Spotting Fake Investors And Predatory Loans

High-cost lenders and scam investors frequently use charm, secrecy, and hurry. Advance-fee loan scams are still prevalent, according to Canadian consumer and anti-fraud authorities. These scams involve organizations advertising easy business funding online and then demanding upfront fees for “insurance,” “processing,” or “assured approval,” after which no loan is ever offered. Even though it is against the law in Ontario for lenders to impose advance fees for loans, victims nonetheless lose thousands of dollars to these scams, particularly if they are in dire need of money or have been turned down by established banks. 

The trend of predatory lending is more widespread. According to Canadian research on women and predatory lending, problems include lenders pressuring women into taking out high-interest installment loans, adding pricey insurance without getting their express approval, and altering terms or costs in the middle of a loan. Payday, installment, rent-to-own, and auto-title lenders are examples of alternative lenders that frequently operate in a regulatory gray area and charge exorbitant effective interest rates and fees that keep borrowers stuck in refinance cycles. Very high annual percentage rates, unclear contracts, early repayment penalties, and pressure to sign hastily without independent advice are all warning signs for businesses.

The Free Money Trap and Fake Grant Scams

The lure of “free money” in the form of grants might be particularly alluring to female founders who are balancing obligations to their families and their businesses. Scammers create websites that seem like official federal or provincial pages, replete with government flags and insignia, and claim unique access to small-business incentives and loans, Canadian authorities warn. These websites frequently charge for “application services” or award lists, or they may even request that business owners open a new bank account in order to get funds. This information could be used for money laundering or may never be utilized to provide actual funding. 

Legitimate government programs typically do not charge fees for access to information, and no commercial organization can promise you government funding, according to a core principle articulated by the Competition Bureau and the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre. Any service that makes claims of guaranteed clearance, uses an official-sounding name, or relies primarily on unconfirmed testimonials should raise suspicion. Women entrepreneurs should verify program titles on official federal or provincial websites before making payments, and, if in doubt, contact the appropriate government agency immediately. 

Smart Due Diligence for Confident Funding Decisions

Due diligence is a two-way street; you should research potential investors as well as your company. Checklists for Canadian investments place strong emphasis on understanding who is funding the venture, how they generate revenue, and the level of control they expect in exchange. Rather than relying on anonymous endorsements, entrepreneurs can begin by verifying the investor’s legal company, registration, and track record. They should look for legitimate portfolio firms, named partners, and independent references. Industry groups, professional networking sites, and public databases can all be used to confirm an investor’s legitimacy and level of activity. 

Ideally, with the assistance of a lawyer or other knowledgeable advisor, founders should review issues such as valuation, dilution, board seats, veto rights, personal guarantees, and repayment plans. Serious warning flags include high-pressure tactics (“sign this week or we walk”), an unwillingness to put important pledges in writing, or resistance to your getting independent legal counsel. Research indicates that misalignment in these areas can lead to long-term friction and risk, so women entrepreneurs may also wish to evaluate congruence in values, governance, and inclusion. An open and honest investor who is prepared to answer challenging questions and review the term sheet in detail is much more likely to become a solid long-term partner. 

Funding Strategies That Reduce Risk

Despite the hazards, women entrepreneurs in Canada have strong funding options, including dedicated programs under the federal Women Entrepreneurship Strategy and the Women Entrepreneurship Loan Fund, which operate through accredited partners rather than unvetted online brokers. Entrepreneurs and women-focused networks recommend starting with reliable sources, such as credit unions, large banks, Community Futures groups, women’s enterprise centers, and verified loan funds, before contemplating higher-cost options. Putting together a strong financial presentation (a clear company model, realistic estimates, and a personal credit plan) increases the likelihood of approval and reduces pressure to accept exploitative terms.

Practical measures include never paying upfront to “unlock” a loan or grant, authenticating lenders and investors through official registries, obtaining all terms in writing, and having a lawyer or trusted advisor examine major deals. Women founders can safeguard their ownership, avoid predatory traps, and still secure the financing they need to develop boldly and sustainably by viewing fundraising as a strategic decision rather than an emergency fix.
