5-leading-pos-systems-for-canadian-resta.title: 5 Leading POS Systems for Canadian Restaurants
5-leading-pos-systems-for-canadian-resta.author: CanadianSME
5-leading-pos-systems-for-canadian-resta.alt: 5 Leading POS Systems for Canadian Restaurants
5-leading-pos-systems-for-canadian-resta.excerpt: Five POS platforms developed and supported in Canada, each built for a different kind of restaurant.
5-leading-pos-systems-for-canadian-resta.html:
*A restaurant’s point-of-sale system is the single piece of technology that processes every order, shift, and dollar. These five platforms are developed and supported in Canada, and each one understands what a Friday night is like.**

Restaurants operate on very tight margins, leaving little space for friction. A server returning to a fixed terminal three times per table, a garbled kitchen ticket, and a card machine that stalls when a party of twelve requests separate bills—all of these cost minutes, and minutes at dinner service add up to covers not turned and labour hours not recovered. As a result, the point-of-sale system has become the single most important technological decision an independent operator makes.

Canadian restaurants also have requirements that global platforms were not meant for. Tip handling and tip-out must align with how Canadian employees are compensated. Interac is not optional. Bilingual service is required in many parts of the country. In Quebec, restaurants must record sales using the provincial sales recording system and issue compliant customer receipts, so the POS system must be designed and certified for that regime rather than altered after the fact.

It’s encouraging that so much of the world’s top restaurant technology is being created here. The five listed below range from a single-location café to a hotel chain with eighty properties. Each is Canadian, promotes local clients, and excels in a different setting.

1. TouchBistro — Toronto, Ontario

*Best for: independent restaurants that want everything in one subscription**

TouchBistro was created in Toronto by people who previously worked in restaurants, and the product still shows this. It is an iPad-based cloud POS geared for the floor rather than the back office, featuring tableside ordering, bespoke floor layouts, bill splitting, menu management, staff permissions, and over 50 reports, as well as offline capability to ensure operation even when the internet is down. The company claims to be Canadian-born and based, with restaurants in over 100 countries.

TouchBistro Payments accepts major credit cards, chip and swipe, and digital wallets such as Apple Pay, Google Pay, and Samsung Pay, integrates with the POS and continues to work during internet outages. Online ordering supports takeout and delivery, with real-time menu sync, integrated payment, and a commission-free DoorDash Drive connection. Reservations handles automatic SMS and email confirmations and reminders, as well as two-way messaging with guests. Gift cards work both online and at the point of sale.

The marketing and earnings tools set it apart from a simple till. Loyalty and CRM provide visitor profiles that feed personalized marketing and repeat-visit promos. Digital invoice capture processes supplier invoices within 48 hours and feeds inventory monitoring, recipe pricing, menu analysis, and budgeting. The kitchen display system processes orders instantly and lets staff tick items off as they go. Restaurants Canada members enjoy a promotional deal on the POS subscription, and support is provided free of charge 24/7, 365 days a year.

2. Lightspeed Restaurant — Montréal, Quebec

*Best for: multi-location groups and operators who live in the data**

Lightspeed Commerce, formed in Montréal in 2005 and listed in both New York and Toronto, is Canada’s most renowned commerce technology business. Lightspeed Restaurant is its hospitality platform: a cloud POS that includes floor layouts and tableside ordering, menu and inventory management, personnel administration, multi-location control, and detailed reporting, with payments built in rather than added on.

Its differentiating feature has always been analytics, and in January 2026 the company introduced Lightspeed AI, a conversational intelligence layer within Lightspeed Restaurant. Instead of creating a report or opening multiple dashboards, an operator can simply ask in plain English which menu items contribute most to margin, where service is bottlenecking, or how performance is trending, and get an answer.

For a group running multiple rooms, the appeal is consolidation and comparison: a single platform across locations, with menus, pricing, and reporting managed centrally while each venue retains the necessary freedom.

3. Squirrel Systems — Burnaby, British Columbia

*Best for: full-service restaurants that want proven reliability**

Squirrel Systems has been serving the restaurant sector for 42 years. Squirrel created one of the first purpose-built restaurant point-of-sale systems in the world, and four decades of experience in full-service dining rooms show in how the product handles the complicated parts — course firing, seat-level ordering, splits and transfers.

Squirrel Cloud is a fully cloud-native platform that eliminates the need for operators to manage mission-critical hardware, software, or data on-site. At the Restaurants Canada Show in March 2026, the company announced menu versioning and scheduling, multi-unit management, all-in-one order and pay on the PAX A6630 handheld, and Squirrel Labour, which combines time and attendance with real-time sales and labour KPI reporting.

Built-in training is the release that will matter most on the floor. With visual menu cues, recipe cards, and upsell prompts integrated into the process, a new server learns the menu while taking orders. Squirrel Pay is a multi-processor app that supports pay-at-table and pay-at-counter and now runs on Moneris Go, with additional Canadian processors scheduled through 2026.

4. SilverWare POS — Markham, Ontario

*Best for: hotels, large venues and multi-revenue operations**

SilverWare POS serves the segment of the market where a restaurant system must do more than just operate a restaurant. Its enterprise platform manages restaurants, bars and lounges, room service, banquet and catering, and retail establishments all under one roof. The company lists approximately 1,000 integration partners in accounting, CRM, inventory, loyalty, payroll, property management, reservations, and CCTV systems.

Oliver & Bonacini Hospitality standardized point-of-sale across 30 restaurants, event spaces, and partner operations in Toronto, Montreal, Calgary, and Edmonton. Regency Hotel Management chose SilverWare to implement point-of-sale across its 82-property portfolio, using table management, mobile payments, property-wide ordering, tableside pay, guestroom ordering via QR code, and portable devices for poolside use. The platform’s GuestX online ordering lets diners order and pay from their phone, and staff training reportedly takes about 45 minutes.

5. PayFacto — Montréal, Québec

*Best for: Quebec restaurants and operators wanting POS and payments from one provider**

PayFacto is the hidden powerhouse of Quebec hospitality technology. Operating in Canada, the United States, and the United Kingdom, the company supports over 10,000 restaurateurs in Quebec alone through two of the country’s most established restaurant POS platforms, Maitre’D and Veloce, which it owns and develops.

The strategic idea is to integrate point-of-sale and payment systems rather than rely on two separate suppliers. PayFacto’s VelPAY handheld combines point-of-sale and payment on a single device: a server takes the order, sends it to the kitchen, and accepts payment at the table without returning to a terminal.

The company strengthened its Quebec presence by acquiring NEOPOS, the province’s largest restaurant POS distributor and systems integrator. For a Quebec operator, that combination is difficult to match: software designed to meet the province’s legal standards, French-language service as standard, and payments handled by the same company that supplies the POS.

At a Glance

  • TouchBistro (Toronto, ON): independent restaurants — everything in one subscription, free 24/7 support, strong profit tools.
  • Lightspeed Restaurant (Montréal, QC): multi-location groups — Lightspeed AI conversational insights, launched January 2026.
  • Squirrel Systems (Burnaby, BC): full-service dining rooms — 42 years in hospitality; 2026 cloud, labour and in-workflow training.
  • SilverWare POS (Markham, ON): hotels and multi-revenue venues — enterprise POS across F&B, banquet and retail; ~1,000 integrations.
  • PayFacto (Montréal, QC): Quebec restaurants — Maitre’D and Veloce plus VelPAY handheld POS and payment in one.

Choosing the Right System

Begin with your service manner, not your cover count. A fast-casual counter, a full-service dining room with courses and seat-level ordering, and a hotel with room service and a banquet hall all require distinctly different systems. Instead of a generic presentation, see one of your own busiest scenarios: a party of ten splitting six ways, a mid-service menu change, or a kitchen printer failing.

Then ask the questions that only matter later. What happens when the internet goes down? What does assistance actually cost, and who responds at 8 p.m. on a Saturday? How does the system handle tips, tip-out, and payroll export? If you operate in Quebec, make sure the system is designed to meet provincial sales recording laws. Also, ask about hardware costs separately from the software.

Finally, weigh the ecosystem just as much as the till. Online ordering, reservations, loyalty, kitchen displays, inventory, and accounting all communicate with the POS, and every integration you avoid saves you an hour of reconciliation. All five companies develop and support their software in Canada, understand Interac, tip management, and bilingual service.

what-happens-to-institutional-knowledge-.title: What Happens to Institutional Knowledge When “That” Employee Leaves
what-happens-to-institutional-knowledge-.author: Rob Nikkel
what-happens-to-institutional-knowledge-.alt: What Happens to Institutional Knowledge When “That” Employee Leaves
what-happens-to-institutional-knowledge-.excerpt: Institutional knowledge shouldn’t live in one person’s head. Why “Ask Jim” isn’t a strategy.
what-happens-to-institutional-knowledge-.html:
*Institutional knowledge shouldn’t live in one person’s head.**

Why “Ask Jim” Isn’t a Strategy

No one notices something until it’s gone. The summer sun is easy to take for granted until it rains. The Wi-Fi is invisible until it goes out. And the go-to person on your team gets relied on for answers right up until the day they can’t be reached.

Every team has one. Let’s call them Jim. Jim has been around long enough that they just know things. Which customer has particular preferences or agreements. Why a certain process gets done a certain way. Who to call when there is a particular fire to put out. None of it is written down anywhere. It’s in Jim’s head.

Then one day, Jim hands in their notice, or retires, or finally takes that long-overdue vacation. What then?

Suddenly, the person everyone routes through can’t be reached. And the scramble that follows isn’t really about backfilling a role or finding coverage. It’s realizing how much institutional knowledge was living in one person’s memory the whole time.

The Knowledge That Never Made It Into a System

Most organizations are good at documenting what’s easy to document: policies, procedures, products/pricing, the org chart. What rarely gets written down is the operational knowledge, the workarounds, the context, the “here’s actually how this works” that accumulates over years on the job.

That knowledge never feels urgent to capture, right up until the person holding it walks out the door. Then it’s gone, and everyone else is left reconstructing it from memory, old emails, and guesswork.

How Your Tech Either Helps or Hinders

Think about how information actually moves through your organization today. Does it live in one centralized place, or is it scattered across shared drives, inboxes, and chat threads with limited visibility or access?

If someone wanted to update a document to reflect how a process actually works now, how easy would that be? Would they know where it lives? Could they make the change themselves, or does it have to go through IT first?

That friction matters because if your systems are hard to update, people stop updating them. And if the information is already hard to contextualize or changes quickly, every extra layer of complexity shrinks the odds it ever gets captured at all.

The more complicated your systems are to navigate, the more likely your team is to take a shortcut instead: an ad hoc folder that gets forgotten, a workaround that only one person understands, or simply going back to asking Jim.

If the official system isn’t the path of least resistance to an answer, your team won’t stay on it for long.

AI Won’t Fix What Was Never Captured

There’s a lot of talk right now about AI helping organizations find information faster, and I think that’s genuinely true. AI is a useful tool for surfacing what an organization already knows.

But AI can’t surface knowledge that was never captured in the first place. It can search a document. It can’t search someone’s head after they’ve left. If the goal is actually protecting institutional knowledge, the work has to happen before it’s missing, not after.

AI is an enablement layer on top of good habits, not a replacement for them.

The Real Cost

People are an organization’s biggest asset; I have always believed that, and this doesn’t change that value. But when institutional knowledge lives in one person, a business isn’t just vulnerable to turnover. It’s slower, more inconsistent, and more dependent on memory than it needs to be. New employees take longer to get up to speed. Customers get different answers depending on who they happen to reach. And every departure, planned or not, becomes a small crisis instead of a normal transition.

Then think about what it’s actually like to be Jim. Think about how much of their day goes to answering the same questions over and over, because the answer has nowhere to live once they give it. Next week, someone else will ask the exact same thing, and the cycle starts again.

Jim deserves their time back too, so they can do work that drives new value, work that actually matters to them and the organization. Or just take the vacation peacefully.

Rob Nikkel is CEO of Intranet Connections (IC), an intranet software company that has spent more than 25 years helping regulated and operations-driven organizations create more connected, informed, and aligned workplaces.

the-growing-pains-of-leadership-why-stro.title: The Growing Pains of Leadership: Why Strong Teams Can’t Depend on One Person
the-growing-pains-of-leadership-why-stro.author: Kal K. Sahota
the-growing-pains-of-leadership-why-stro.alt: The Growing Pains of Leadership: Why Strong Teams Can’t Depend on One Person
the-growing-pains-of-leadership-why-stro.excerpt: Building a team that can grow means giving people the confidence, support and opportunity to lead.
the-growing-pains-of-leadership-why-stro.html:
*Building a team that can grow means creating an environment where people have the confidence, support, and opportunity to lead.**

In the early stages of building a team, it’s natural to be involved in almost everything. You know your people, understand the work, and can quickly step in when something needs attention. For many leaders, being hands-on is simply part of getting the business off the ground.

But as an organization grows, that same approach doesn’t always serve the team as well. You’ll notice small shifts. People wait for direction instead of moving forward. Decisions keep landing back on the same desks. Team leads become the link between teams that should simply be working with each other. Over time, progress depends less on the strength of the team and more on whether a few key people are available.

That doesn’t mean you have the wrong people. It could simply mean that the organization has outgrown the way it’s been operating.

In my experience, one of the hardest parts of leadership is recognizing when the approach that got you here won’t get you where you want to go.

Growth Requires a Different Kind of Leadership

Smaller teams, as a byproduct, work really closely together. You watch how one another operates; you learn and pick things up through everyday tasks and activities.

But over time, teams grow and bandwidth starts to stretch the quality time leaders can offer individual team members. With less opportunity for face time and ad hoc discussions, team members develop their own ways of working. This is a good thing, but only if you set them up for success.

The best leaders not only share openly what’s next, but more importantly, the ‘why’ and the reasoning that brought them to that decision. That’s how you authentically transfer knowledge and share your style of leadership. Team members can take what resonates with them and develop their own style, equally as powerful but tailored to who they are.

Leading by example has become more of a catch phrase over the years. But it is a very powerful way to lead if you take the time and invest in your team. Share the anecdotes, the reasons why, and the different options you considered. That instills confidence when team members are faced with similar situations.

What does that look like in practice? Be clear about priorities and show your team how their work connects to the bigger picture. Give them space to make decisions within their roles. They may not tackle things exactly as you would, but give them the space to figure it out. Coach by empowering and be available when there are breakdowns. Show no judgment. The best learning happens in the breakdowns, and the best leaders coach and guide you through them. That last part is harder than it sounds.

If you do this well, the team members you coach will become powerful leaders. When you no longer have the capacity to be in every room or conversation, your team members are empowered to pick up where you leave off.

Recognize the People Who Make Others Better

Most organizations have a few people who consistently go above and beyond. They solve problems, support team members, take work off leaders’ plates, remember the details, and step in whenever something needs doing. Those people deserve recognition. But as leaders, we need to be mindful not to create a culture where success depends too heavily on a few individuals.

When one person becomes the unofficial owner of a process, a relationship, or a decision, the organization may benefit in the short term. Over time, that dependency can limit everyone involved. That person has less room to take on new challenges, their team members have fewer opportunities to build their own expertise, and the organization becomes vulnerable whenever that person is away or moves on.

It’s worth paying just as much attention to the people who make the whole team better. Who’s sharing what they’ve learned? Who’s mentoring new employees? Who’s building the processes that make everyone’s work easier? Who’s committed to raising the bar for the whole team?

Those contributions may be less visible than being the person everyone turns to when something goes wrong, but they build something more valuable over time: a team that continues to grow stronger with every new person who joins it.

Build a Team That Can Grow Together

Having talented people on your team is critical, but building a strong team takes more than that. They need the right tools, access to information, and the trust to make decisions together without waiting for a team lead to step in and guide them.

When people spend too much time tracking down information, waiting for answers, or working around silos between departments, progress slows. As leaders, part of our responsibility is to remove those barriers and make it easier for people to work together and do their best work.

As organizations grow, there will always be unexpected challenges, shifting priorities, and people stepping into new roles. You can’t prevent change. What you can do is build a team that’s equipped to adapt to it.

That changes the question we ask ourselves as leaders. Less “How do I make sure everything gets done?” and more “Am I building a team that can succeed without depending on me, or any one person?”

For me, that’s what leadership looks like as an organization grows. Less about being the person everyone needs. More about giving people the confidence, context, and support to achieve more together than any one of them could alone.

Kal K. Sahota is Chief Growth Officer at Intranet Connections, with more than three decades of leadership experience spanning SaaS, financial services, and organizational transformation.

making-cross-border-money-work-harder-fo.title: Making Cross-Border Money Work Harder for Canadian SMEs
making-cross-border-money-work-harder-fo.author: Maheen Bari
making-cross-border-money-work-harder-fo.alt: Making Cross-Border Money Work Harder for Canadian SMEs
making-cross-border-money-work-harder-fo.excerpt: Jackee Wong, Fractional CMO at Keytom, on why payment speed, transparency and predictability matter for SMEs working across markets.
making-cross-border-money-work-harder-fo.html:
In an exclusive interview with CanadianSME Small Business Magazine, Jackee Wong, Fractional CMO at Keytom, explores how modern financial technology can help Canadian SMEs navigate the growing complexities of cross-border payments. Drawing from years of international experience across technology, cybersecurity, fintech, and PayFi, Jackee shares why payment speed, transparency, and predictability matter so much for businesses operating across markets.

*Interview by Maheen Bari**

Jackee Wong is a 3rd-generation Chinese Canadian, failed entrepreneur and tech growth executive who has spent 11+ years helping international brands grow across consumer internet, cybersecurity, Fintech and PayFi. He currently works out of Hong Kong as Fractional CMO at Keytom.

You have worked across global technology, cybersecurity, PayFi, and consumer-internet brands. What brought you to Keytom, and what problem do you believe the platform can help solve for Canadians and businesses managing money across borders?

I’ve worked internationally for most of my career, so moving money across borders has always been part of my life. But a car accident made the issue much more personal.

I was hit by a car while crossing the road. During recovery, my medical expenses exceeded the fiat funds I had readily available. When I tried to pay with crypto, I ran into delays and friction exactly when speed and predictability mattered most.

That’s why Keytom’s focus on reducing friction around how people move and use money resonated with me. The team’s approach mattered too. They adapted interviews and onboarding around my rehabilitation and rest, making it easier to join while I continued recovering.

At Keytom, we bring traditional currencies and supported crypto into one app, with payment cards where available. For Canadians and businesses working internationally, the aim is to make receiving, converting and spending money simpler.

Traditional cross-border payments can include fixed fees, foreign-exchange costs, and delays that disproportionately affect freelancers, contractors, and SMEs making smaller transactions. Why do these costs matter so much for smaller businesses?

A fixed fee on a US$100,000 payment is easy to overlook. Take that same fee out of US$500, and you notice it. I sometimes work on hourly consulting agreements, with payments between $400 and $900. Traditional bank-transfer fees can take a real bite out of those amounts.

Smaller businesses often don’t have the same cash reserves as large enterprises. Many are founder-led, so when a payment costs more than expected, the founder may end up covering the gap personally.

That is why I think providers should design for predictability. A business should know what it will pay, what the recipient will receive, and when the money will arrive. I don’t think enough providers make those basics clear.

At Keytom, we focus on keeping fixed fees very low and pricing transparent. The total cost still depends on the payment method and any currency conversion, so customers need to see the whole picture. The point is simple: founders should be able to price a payment before they send it.

How do delayed international payments affect day-to-day operations and working capital, and what practical difference can faster settlement make for SMEs operating across markets?

I’ve founded three businesses, and getting money in and out was consistently one of the biggest problems.

Startups need to spend money to make money, often with very little cash to spare. I had clients in Argentina who wanted to pay but struggled to get the money to me. In 2025, I had the reverse problem paying a contractor who had moved from the Middle East to Uzbekistan.

In both cases, the willingness to pay was there. Getting the payment through was the blocker.

That creates a working-capital gap. Contractors still need paying, work still needs funding, and the founder often has to bridge the difference. Inevitably, that slows growth.

Faster settlement can shorten the cash-conversion cycle, bringing forward the point when money comes back into the business. More predictable arrival times also make it easier to plan the next expense. For Canadian SMEs, that means being better equipped to work with customers and suppliers in more countries. It can support growth beyond the U.S. market and reduce dependence on it.

Why is reliable, practical access to money so important for people who travel, work internationally, or operate across borders—and what should users consider when choosing a financial platform?

I think access to your money should work 24/7. Unexpected payment blocks are bad enough. Not being able to resolve them is worse.

A few months ago, I was in Singapore on business when my bank stopped a credit card payment. I couldn’t challenge the block at the time, and it disrupted the trip. Thankfully, I had another way to pay. That experience changed what I look for in a financial platform.

First, compliance. Keytom’s Canadian entity is registered as a Money Services Business with FINTRAC in Canada, and we use fast, automated identity checks as part of onboarding.

Then, usability. Fees should be clear. Settlement should be as fast as possible where supported. And users should know exactly which countries, currencies and payment methods are actually available to them.

And one practical lesson from me: always keep a backup payment option. I was very glad I had one.

Keytom has recently introduced CAD business accounts for Canadian companies. What opportunities does this create, and what final advice would you share with entrepreneurs managing international payments?

For a Canadian business, “global” still has to work locally. That is where CAD business accounts become useful. Companies can manage Canadian dollars alongside other supported currencies and digital assets in one place.

The bigger opportunity is choice. Better cross-border financial tools can make it more practical for Canadian SMEs to work with customers, contractors and suppliers beyond Canada and the U.S.

When choosing a provider, I would focus on transparency, reliability and strong local payment capabilities. Don’t stop at the lowest advertised transfer fee. Check the FX rate, other charges, how long the payment takes, and whether the recipient can actually use the money locally.

A payment isn’t finished when it is sent. It’s finished when the other side can use it.

The views and opinions expressed in this interview are those of the interviewee and do not necessarily reflect the official policy or position of CanadianSME Small Business Magazine.

unlocking-growth-through-government-fund.title: Unlocking Growth Through Government Funding and Advisory Programs
unlocking-growth-through-government-fund.author: SK Uddin
unlocking-growth-through-government-fund.alt: Unlocking Growth Through Government Funding and Advisory Programs
unlocking-growth-through-government-fund.excerpt: Government assistance can benefit Canadian SMEs — but only when it is matched to a specific company need.
unlocking-growth-through-government-fund.html:
Government assistance can benefit Canadian small and medium-sized businesses, but only when it is tailored to a specific company need. A founder looking for startup funding requires a different program than a manufacturing company purchasing equipment, a technology business commercializing an innovation, or an established company planning to enter a new export market. The idea is to view public support as an extension of a business plan rather than a replacement for one.

Funding programs can be competitive, applications take time, and eligibility rules may change. However, a well-prepared SME can leverage funding, advisory services, and export help to mitigate risk, create capability, and advance growth projects.

Start With the Right Need

Before seeking a grant or loan, business owners should identify the specific objective they want to achieve. Is the company purchasing equipment, developing a product, increasing productivity, hiring employees, entering a foreign market, implementing technology, or addressing a short-term cash-flow gap? This clarity decides the type of support to seek.

A financing scheme may be more appropriate for purchasing assets such as machinery, vehicles, or leasehold improvements. An innovation program may concentrate on research, development, or commercialization. Export support might be used to fund market research, trade shows, or the adaptation of sales materials for international consumers. A great application begins with a clear business case: what the project is, why it matters, how much it will cost, what the company will contribute, and how the outcome will produce value.

Canada Small Business Financing Program

The Canada Small Business Financing Program (CSBFP) assists Canadian small businesses in obtaining finance that would otherwise be unavailable or supplied only on less favourable terms. It is distributed through participating financial institutions rather than directly by a federal department. For an SME, the program may be useful for financing equipment, technology, leasehold improvements, or other qualified business assets.

Owners should provide a participating lender with current financial statements, tax information, revenue estimates, asset appraisals, and a clear explanation of repayment capacity. Don’t approach finance as a vague plea for money. Present a plan outlining how the asset will enhance capacity, reduce expenses, improve service, or produce more income.

Business Development Bank of Canada

The Business Development Bank of Canada (BDC) provides financing and advising services to Canadian entrepreneurs. It might be a valuable choice for organizations that require working capital, equipment financing, growth capital, technology investment, or assistance with a specific expansion plan. According to the federal government, qualifying small enterprises can apply online through BDC for funding of up to $350,000 with flexible payback terms.

Before applying, owners should gather current financial records, a forecast, a description of the investment, and proof of market demand. Advisory services can also help organizations clarify their strategy, improve operations, and prepare for lender conversations.

Regional Development Agencies

Businesses in Canada can access programs tailored to local economic conditions, industry strengths, and regional priorities through regional development agencies. These include the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency, Canada Economic Development for Quebec Regions, FedDev Ontario, PrairiesCan, PacifiCan, CanNor, and the Federal Economic Development Agency for Northern Ontario.

Their projects may support productivity, innovation, clean growth, tourism, local economic development, corporate expansion, and regional supply chain resilience. Because program availability varies by geography and policy priorities, owners should contact the agency serving their region as soon as possible rather than waiting until a deadline approaches.

The Regional Tariff Response Initiative, which offers $1 billion over three years to support SMEs affected by tariffs, aims to boost productivity, cut costs, strengthen supply networks, and establish new markets.

Innovation Support and IRAP

Businesses developing or enhancing products, processes, or technologies should seek innovation-focused support rather than relying solely on operating cash flow. The National Research Council of Canada’s Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC IRAP) provides innovative SMEs with advisory services and, in some cases, financial assistance for technology and innovation projects.

Innovation support is most useful when a company can clearly define the technical problem, market opportunity, project timetable, expected commercial returns, and internal capacity to accomplish the work. It is not exclusive to software firms. Manufacturers, clean-tech companies, food producers, health innovators, and specialized service providers may all have qualifying innovation projects.

Export Support Through CanExport

Exporting can lessen reliance on a single customer base or domestic market, but expansion entails risk. Market research, legal counsel, travel, trade trips, local alliances, and customized marketing materials can all be costly before the first sale is made. CanExport SMEs, administered by Canada’s Trade Commissioner Service, provides competitive funding to eligible Canadian SMEs seeking to expand into new overseas markets.

Successful candidates could receive up to $50,000 for approved international business development activities. For the 2026-27 program year, eligibility conditions include being a Canadian for-profit incorporated firm, limited liability partnership, or cooperative with at least three full-time employees and a minimum annual revenue of $300,000. Funding is limited and not guaranteed.

Provincial and Local Complements

Federal programs are just one aspect of the support environment. Provincial and territorial governments, municipalities, local chambers of commerce, business improvement areas, community futures organizations, incubators, accelerators, and post-secondary schools may provide finance, mentoring, export support, training, or sector-specific services.

Local groups often know which initiatives are currently active, which applications are due soon, and what funders expect of candidates in a given region. Owners can start with the federal Business Benefits Finder, a searchable website that helps firms find government programs and services based on their region, industry, and growth needs.

How to Submit a Strong Application

Successful applications are typically specific, comprehensive, and supported by evidence. Avoid broad terms like “growth” or “innovation.” Instead, say what the company will do, how much it will cost, when it will happen, who will do the work, and what measurable results can be expected. Include financial figures, supplier quotations, sales estimates, customer evidence, team bios, and the company’s own contribution where needed.

Before committing to any expenses, read the requirements carefully and make sure they are eligible. Many programs require approval before project expenses are incurred. For export funding, the Trade Commissioner Service suggests applying at least 60 business days before the first proposed activity.

Support Works Best With Strategy

Government assistance is most useful when it expedites a smart business decision. Canadian SMEs should start with a clear need, select the best source of financing or assistance, create credible documentation, and adhere to program guidelines.

Whether the goal is to buy equipment, develop an innovative product, establish a regional supply chain, or enter a new export market, the most successful entrepreneurs use support programs to make a viable strategy more attainable — not to substitute for the discipline required to carry it out.

helping-canadian-smes-embrace-ai-without.title: Helping Canadian SMEs Embrace AI Without Data Security Risks
helping-canadian-smes-embrace-ai-without.author: SK Uddin
helping-canadian-smes-embrace-ai-without.alt: Helping Canadian SMEs Embrace AI Without Data Security Risks
helping-canadian-smes-embrace-ai-without.excerpt: Generative AI can save Canadian SMEs time. How to adopt it without exposing client files, contracts or customer data.
helping-canadian-smes-embrace-ai-without.html:
Generative artificial intelligence can assist Canadian small and medium-sized businesses in creating content, summarizing documents, responding to common customer inquiries, organizing notes, and reducing time spent on repeated tasks. However, its convenience can lead to new concerns. Employees who enter a client file, financial spreadsheet, legal contract, or confidential proposal into an unapproved AI tool risk exposing sensitive information without recognizing it.

The correct strategy is not to entirely ban AI or to enable unlimited use. It is to develop a practical policy that includes approving appropriate technologies, categorizing information, training personnel, maintaining human review, and tracking how AI is used. In Canada, enterprises remain responsible for their privacy and security standards, even when they use an independent AI vendor. The Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada issues recommendations to organizations on applying privacy standards to generative AI technologies.

Begin With an Approved-Tools Policy

The first question for an SME is straightforward: which AI products are suitable for business use? Without a clear answer, employees may use free consumer products on their own, register accounts with personal email addresses, and upload company information to platforms that the organization cannot monitor or control.

An approved-tools policy should specify which AI services staff may use, the permissible uses for each tool, and the types of information that must never be entered. It should also specify who can approve a new tool and who owns the company’s account.

For example, a marketing team may be permitted to use an approved AI provider to generate social media caption ideas based on publicly available information. It should not use the same tool to paste an unpublished product roadmap, customer list, or confidential campaign strategy unless it has been reviewed and approved.

Classify Data Before It Leaves the Business

Data classification is the foundation for safe AI use. Employees can’t make good decisions about sharing information unless they understand how sensitive it is. Small businesses can start with four practical categories:

  • Public: materials already published, such as website copy, press announcements, and approved product descriptions.
  • Internal: routine operating information that is not made public but would do minimal harm if released.
  • Confidential: pricing, sales estimates, supplier terms, contracts, company strategy, and intellectual property.
  • Personal or sensitive: customer, employee, or applicant information, payment details, health information, identity documents, and private correspondence.

As a general rule, public information can be used in approved AI technologies. Internal information may need approval. Confidential and personal information should not be input until the business has completed the necessary legal, privacy, security, and vendor assessments. Under Canada’s federal private-sector privacy law, companies may collect, use, and disclose personal information only for legitimate and essential purposes.

Keep Humans Responsible for Decisions

AI can generate valuable drafts, summaries, and suggestions, but it can also produce inaccurate, incomplete, or biased results. A confident tone does not necessarily imply a correct answer. Canadian SMEs should require human review before sending AI-generated content to a customer, using it in a contract or financial correspondence, or relying on it for employment, legal, safety, or eligibility decisions.

The reviewer should verify facts, calculations, tone, citations, confidentiality, and compliance with company policies — the more significant the choice, the greater the need for human oversight. A customer service representative may use AI to draft a response to a common inquiry, but a trained person should still double-check pricing, delivery obligations, and any product claims before sending it.

Protect Customer Data by Design

Customer information should never be viewed as free material for experimentation. Before implementing AI in a chatbot, customer care workflow, or marketing process, a company should decide what information will be collected, why it is needed, where it will be stored, and who will have access to it. The Office of the Privacy Commissioner’s business guidance explains obligations under PIPEDA, including consent, safeguards, breaches, and outsourcing.

Use only the information needed to complete the task. Whenever possible, remove names, account numbers, contact information, and other identifiers from data before testing or drafting. When an AI system is used in a service encounter or decision-making process, customers should be given clear information.

Vet AI Vendors Before Deployment

An AI provider is more than just a software supplier. It might become a component of the company’s information security and privacy environment. Before subscribing, owners should ask what happens to prompts, uploaded files, and generated outputs.

  • Is the provider using client material to train its models?
  • Can the business turn off model training or data retention?
  • Where is the data processed and stored?
  • Does the provider offer business accounts with access controls and audit logs?
  • How is data protected in transit and at rest?
  • How does the organization export or remove data?
  • What notice will the provider issue if a security event occurs?

The Canadian Centre for Cyber Security recommends that organizations using third-party suppliers ensure those suppliers implement strong cybersecurity safeguards.

Limit Permissions and Protect Accounts

AI platforms should be handled just like any other business-critical service. Use centrally controlled accounts rather than personal subscriptions, enforce multi-factor authentication, and grant staff only the access required for their roles. Not everyone needs the ability to build new integrations, invite external users, connect to corporate data sources, or view usage logs.

Limit administrator access to a small group of trusted individuals, and review permissions when employees change roles or leave the company. Strong access control is especially necessary when AI connects to email, cloud storage, CRM systems, knowledge bases, or customer-service platforms.

Train Employees on Real Scenarios

AI policy documents are only useful when employees understand how to use them. Training should use brief, realistic examples: “Can I paste this customer email into the AI tool?” “Can I have the tool summarize this contract?” “May I use an AI-generated answer without verifying it?” Teach employees to recognize confidential and personal information, use only approved platforms, and report any concerns to a manager or privacy contact.

AI-generated phishing, fake audio or video, and erroneous outputs should also be covered. The Canadian Centre for Cyber Security recommends building internal expertise and providing clear guidelines on the responsible use of AI tools, including handling sensitive information.

Keep Records and Improve Continuously

An SME does not need a sophisticated governance framework, but it should be able to show how it handles AI. Maintain a basic list of permitted tools, including the owner, purpose, data categories, vendor agreements, authorized users, and review dates.

Record key choices such as why a tool was allowed, what data is restricted, when staff were trained, and how an incident will be reported. Review the register every quarter or whenever the company introduces a new AI feature.

Use AI With Control, Not Fear

Canadian SMEs can benefit from generative AI while maintaining customer confidence and company confidentiality. The practical approach is to carefully approve tools, categorize data, restrict permissions, validate results, train people, and document decisions.

AI should help people do better work, not push firms to share information they would never reveal by email or in public. With clear safeguards in place, SMEs can pursue productivity gains while remaining accountable for their most important data and decisions.

preparing-canadian-businesses-for-cyber-.title: Preparing Canadian Businesses for Cyber Risks: Ransomware and Fraud Threats
preparing-canadian-businesses-for-cyber-.author: Kripa Anand
preparing-canadian-businesses-for-cyber-.alt: Preparing Canadian Businesses for Cyber Risks: Ransomware and Fraud Threats
preparing-canadian-businesses-for-cyber-.excerpt: Cyber insurance can help an SME recover from ransomware or fraud — but insurers expect preparation first.
preparing-canadian-businesses-for-cyber-.html:
Cyber insurance can assist a Canadian small- or medium-sized organization in recovering from a ransomware attack, a fraud incident, or a data breach. Still, it is not a replacement for cybersecurity planning. Insurers increasingly expect firms to demonstrate that they have taken reasonable precautions to protect their systems before an incident happens. If an owner is unable to show how accounts are safeguarded, backups are tested, or personnel are trained, acquiring coverage may become more difficult, and claims may face increased scrutiny.

The practical goal is to be “evidence ready.” Before applying for or renewing cyber insurance, a company should understand what technology it owns, what data it stores, who has access to it, how the firm would restore operations, and who to call in the early hours of an incident. The Canadian Centre for Cyber Security identifies strong controls, such as multi-factor authentication and recoverable backups, as critical strategies for reducing ransomware risk.

Understand What Insurance Does

Cyber insurance is intended to help manage the financial and operational damage that may result from an incident. Depending on the policy, coverage may include incident response services, forensic investigations, legal counsel, customer notification, data restoration, business interruption, cyber extortion, and liability claims. However, coverage, limits, exclusions, deductibles, and notification requirements differ widely between insurers and policies.

Owners should review their insurance with a broker or qualified advisor before an incident, not after one. Ask which events are covered, which security procedures are required, whether social engineering fraud is covered, how quickly the insurer must be notified, and which legal, forensic, or incident-response providers to engage. The Insurance Bureau of Canada has released a guide to help SMEs understand the role cyber insurance can play in recovery.

Create an Asset and Data Inventory

A firm cannot protect or insure something it does not understand. Begin by identifying the systems that keep things running: email, cloud storage, accounting and payroll platforms, online banking, websites, e-commerce systems, point-of-sale terminals, customer databases, employee devices, servers, routers, and third-party software. Then identify the information stored in each system.

Label the assets that are critical to everyday operations and those that hold sensitive or regulated information. A spreadsheet listing the system owner, provider, data type, administrator account, recovery method, and renewal date is a valuable starting point for risk assessments, insurance applications, and incident response.

Enforce MFA Across Critical Accounts

Multi-factor authentication (MFA) is one of the most significant security measures a Canadian SME can deploy. It adds a second layer of verification beyond a password, preventing an attacker from accessing an account even after obtaining login credentials through phishing or password reuse. The Canadian Centre for Cyber Security advocates phishing-resistant MFA and strong, unique passphrases for all accounts and devices.

Enable MFA first for email, remote access, cloud administration, accounting, payroll, online banking, domain registration, and backup management accounts. An insurer may ask whether MFA is simply available or mandatory for all users, so keep records of which accounts are covered, when enforcement began, and who handles exceptions.

Test Backups Before You Need Them

A backup is only useful if it can be restored. Ransomware operators frequently attempt to encrypt, remove, or disable backups before demanding payment. Businesses should keep multiple copies of vital data and ensure that at least one is protected from routine network access or unauthorized deletion.

Document what is backed up, how frequently it runs, where copies are stored, who has access, and the results of restore tests. A brief record of a successful recovery test may be more valuable to an insurer — and the business — than a verbal assurance that backups exist.

Train Employees to Stop Fraud

Many cyber incidents begin with a deceptively simple message: a forged invoice, an urgent request from a senior executive, a fraudulent payment-change alert, or a link that impersonates a trusted provider. Employees who handle payments, wages, customer data, and email are critical to managing risk.

Staff should be able to identify malicious links and attachments, verify banking changes using a known phone number, report suspicious requests, and never share passwords or MFA codes. Make it clear that reporting a suspected mistake promptly is encouraged. Keep attendance records, phishing test results, and policy copies to show that awareness is ongoing.

Retain Records and Evidence

Documentation saves time when applying for insurance or reporting an incident. Maintain a secure, up-to-date record of software subscriptions, hardware, user and administrator accounts, service providers, insurance details, security measures, and key business contacts.

Useful evidence includes MFA enforcement reports, access reviews, patching records, backup reports, restore test results, training records, vendor security questionnaires, and a basic system diagram. Good records let owners answer insurer questions accurately and help incident-response experts understand the environment faster.

Build an Incident-Response Contact List

The first hours of an incident are often confusing. Owners should decide in advance who has authority to act and where to seek help. A contact list should include the cyber insurer’s 24-hour reporting line, insurance broker, managed IT provider, legal counsel, privacy adviser, bank fraud contact, key software vendors, and the leadership team.

Keep a printed copy in a secure location, as the company may be unable to access email or cloud documents during an attack.

Review Vendors and Client Requirements

Many SMEs rely on third-party providers for payroll, payments, e-commerce, cloud storage, customer service, and IT support. A vendor’s weakness can cause interruption or privacy issues. Before signing a contract, ask suppliers about MFA, access controls, data storage, backups, incident notification, and data export options.

Some clients, particularly larger corporations and public-sector buyers, may require proof of cybersecurity policies or insurance before awarding work. A documented security program can build trust with customers, partners, and insurers.

Insurance Follows Preparation

Preparing for cyber insurance is best done before a ransomware message, fraudulent transfer, or data breach occurs. Canadian SMEs should begin with a concise asset inventory, enforced MFA, tested backups, trained personnel, accurate records, vetted vendors, and a defined response plan.

These steps limit interruption, maintain customer trust, and strengthen the company’s ability to recover. Insurance can be a valuable financial safety net, but planning is the foundation for recovery.

the-cra-registration-change-that-depends.title: The CRA Registration Change That Depends On Whether You Have Filed
the-cra-registration-change-that-depends.author: Bashar Qawas
the-cra-registration-change-that-depends.alt: The CRA Registration Change That Depends On Whether You Have Filed
the-cra-registration-change-that-depends.excerpt: Business Registration Online now requires a CRA account — and creating one depends on having a recently assessed tax return.
the-cra-registration-change-that-depends.html:
Business Registration Online now requires a CRA account. If you need to create one, outside Alberta and British Columbia that depends on having a recently assessed personal income tax return.

Since July 14, 2026, Business Registration Online has only been accessible through a CRA account. That is the service used to get a business number, open payroll, or add a program account to a business number you already have.

For most owners this is a minor change. Sign in, register, and your accounts are issued immediately. If you already have a CRA account, you carry on using it as before.

The obstacle is for owners who do not yet have one and need to create it. There, the deciding factor is not the age or size of the business. It is whether the individual owner or director has an assessed personal income tax return from within the last two years.

What the change actually gates

You do not use Business Registration Online to incorporate, but where the business number comes from depends on where you incorporate.

With federal incorporation, and with incorporation or registration in the eight participating provinces, a business number is assigned as part of that process. If you incorporate in Newfoundland and Labrador, the Northwest Territories, Nunavut, Quebec or Yukon, you obtain the business number from the CRA separately, and that is a step this change now sits in front of.

Everywhere else the requirement arrives at the following step, when you open a program account.

Either way, new sole proprietors registering for the first time and established owners adding payroll or GST/HST for the first time now need a CRA account before they can use BRO.

The phone route is gone as well. For routine registrations the CRA now directs everything through BRO, with a small set of published exceptions covered below.

One regional point worth knowing: Business Registration Online covers GST/HST registration for the rest of the country but not for businesses in Quebec. Those registrations are handled separately.

The eligibility requirement

To register for a new CRA account using CRA credentials or a Sign-In Partner, you are asked for figures from your most recent assessed income tax and benefit return, and that return needs to be from within the last two years. A return you filed last week but that has not been assessed yet may not get you through. The CRA directs anyone who has never filed, or has not filed within that window, to a different route entirely. This applies to creating the account, not to using one you already have.

That describes more people than it first appears. Newcomers to Canada starting a business in their first year here. Someone returning after several years abroad with no recent Canadian return. Anyone whose last two years produced no filing obligation they acted on.

Alberta and British Columbia are the exception. You may register through a provincial partner even if you have never filed taxes, using an Alberta.ca Account or a BC Services Card, and that route can give immediate access without document verification or a mailed security code.

What to do if you cannot open an account

The CRA publishes an answer to this, though it sits at the end of the announcement.

Form RC1, Request for a Business Number and Certain Program Accounts, is the designated route if you have never filed your taxes, if you have not filed in the last two years, or if you cannot otherwise meet the CRA account registration requirements. It is a mail-in form rather than an online alternative, so build the extra time into your planning rather than treating it as equivalent.

It covers a business number and certain program accounts, not every account type, so confirm the specific accounts you need are included.

If you can open an account, do it before you need it

Registering with CRA credentials or a Sign-In Partner requires verifying your identity, and there are two routes.

The document verification service uses a mobile device and gives immediate access. The alternative is a CRA security code, which the CRA mails to the address on file within 10 business days. The CRA recommends the first over the second, and the reason is timing.

You will also enrol in two multi-factor authentication options for receiving a one-time passcode.

The timing is what catches people out. Set the account up while nothing depends on it.

Other situations the online route does not cover

Business Registration Online also cannot be used to reactivate a previously closed program account, register a business owned by another business such as a corporate or partnership partner, register where the owner or director is deceased and an estate needs to file, or register a Canadian business with only non-resident owners.

Confirm your situation is a standard registration before assuming the online path applies.

The practical summary

  • If you already have a CRA account, sign in and carry on.
  • If you do not have one and you have an assessed return from within the last two years, set it up now and use document verification rather than waiting on a mailed code.
  • If you do not have an account and have no assessed return from the last two years, or have never filed in Canada, do not wait at the online door. In Alberta or British Columbia, a provincial partner sign-in can get you in immediately. Everywhere else, Form RC1 is the route, and because it goes by mail it needs to be started well before the date you need the accounts open.

Bashar Qawas is a partner at Better Books Canada, a bookkeeping and tax firm in Ottawa, and a former auditor with the Canada Revenue Agency.

top-5-business-internet-providers-for-sm.title: Top 5 Business Internet Providers for Small Businesses in Canada
top-5-business-internet-providers-for-sm.author: CanadianSME
top-5-business-internet-providers-for-sm.alt: Top 5 Business Internet Providers for Small Businesses in Canada
top-5-business-internet-providers-for-sm.excerpt: The internet has quietly become a small business’s most important piece of infrastructure. Five Canadian carriers, from Vancouver to Halifax, keeping small companies running.
top-5-business-internet-providers-for-sm.html:
*The internet has quietly become a small business’s most important piece of infrastructure, and it is typically purchased solely on price. These five Canadian carriers, from Vancouver to Halifax, are establishing networks to keep the country’s small companies running.**

Every small business owner has experienced this: the connection goes down, and nothing works for a few minutes. The payment terminal, cloud accounting, booking system, phones, and video conference with the client who flew in for the event. In a country where a growing share of small business revenue comes from software, internet connectivity has shifted from an overhead line item to the foundation on which everything else is built.

That is why a business connection differs from a home connection, even if the speeds look the same on paper. A business plan actually buys upload speed that matches download speed — critical for video calls, cloud backups, and sending large files — as well as service commitments, static IP addresses where needed, priority support queues staffed during business hours and beyond, and the option of a backup connection that takes over automatically when the primary one fails.

Canada’s market has an extremely good balance of national carriers with significant fibre investment, provincial providers with coverage that nationals cannot match, and independents establishing their own networks in congested urban areas. One practical note: business internet availability in Canada is determined by address rather than city. Two businesses on the same street may have completely different options depending on what is built into each building, so the best approach is to check your specific address with two or three of the suppliers listed below.

1. TELUS Business — Vancouver, British Columbia

*Best for: businesses in Western Canada wanting fibre plus everything else**

TELUS has structured its business case around PureFibre, a 100% fibre-to-the-premises network where fibre runs all the way to the enterprise connection point rather than stopping at a neighbourhood cabinet. The practical effect is symmetrical speed and consistency — the connection does not slow down when the entire street is online at four o’clock. In Alberta alone, over 1.2 million homes and businesses now have PureFibre connection, with over 120,000 in rural regions.

The business line-up ranges from Fibre Internet 300 to 1G, 1.5G, and 3G, with a Business Wi-Fi access point and Wi-Fi 6 integrated across all tiers. The most notable feature is TELUS Internet Backup, an automatic wireless failover that takes over if the fibre connection breaks, costing roughly $20 per month over a three-year period. TELUS also packages business mobility, cloud phone, security, and IT services from a single provider and bill, and now offers three months of free connectivity when you purchase qualified PureFibre Internet, Business Wi-Fi, and mobility together.

The network is continually increasing, frequently in collaboration. TELUS announced PureFibre for the Calgary-Bonavista community in April 2026, in collaboration with Fibre Connect and Ledcor, and it has invested heavily in bringing PureFibre to regional Quebec communities in partnership with the federal and provincial governments. PureFibre is also 85% more energy efficient than copper and more resistant to adverse weather — and TELUS directly supports the small business sector through its Stand With Owners program.

2. SaskTel — Regina, Saskatchewan

*Best for: Saskatchewan businesses, including well outside the cities**

For nearly 120 years, SaskTel has built the networks that connect Saskatchewan, and as a provincial Crown corporation, it bases its investment decisions on the province rather than a national footprint. That shows up where it matters for small businesses: in the towns and rural communities that larger carriers neglect. The corporation recorded $1.398 billion in sales and $104.7 million in net income for fiscal year 2025-26, with $443.3 million in total capital investment reinvested in Saskatchewan.

Its fibre network, infiNET, provides up to 5 gigabits per second for business users, with symmetrical options available, unlimited consumption, and 24/7 service. Where fibre has not yet reached, Business internet and Business interNET Extended keep smaller communities connected. Contracted business rates are available on one-, three-, and five-year terms; a wireless backup add-on protects against outages, and SaskTel bundles cybersecurity services alongside connectivity — vulnerability scanning, quarterly consultation, security eLearning, and phishing simulation.

Since launching infiNET in 2011, SaskTel has committed approximately $1 billion to connecting Saskatchewan homes and companies. As of March 2026, the network had reached 194 municipalities, with fibre accessible to 81% of homes and businesses. Its Rural Fibre Initiative pledges $280 million to provide infiNET to over 200 rural towns by the end of 2027, bringing coverage to around 85% of the province.

3. Beanfield — Toronto, Ontario

*Best for: urban businesses that want an independent network and no surprises**

Dan Armstrong founded Beanfield in 1988 in a Toronto neighbourhood the huge incumbent telco had overlooked, where small businesses struggled for access just as the internet was taking off. Beanfield established a fibre network throughout the neighbourhood, and the company has expanded ever since.

Beanfield now develops, builds, owns, and runs its own fibre-optic network, rather than reselling someone else’s, with over 500 employees and connections to over 3,600 commercial and residential buildings in Toronto, Montreal, Vancouver, and Ottawa. Symmetrical speeds can exceed 8 Gbps, and all plans include unlimited bandwidth, free installation, and hardware rental at no additional cost — with no long-term commitment, a two-year price guarantee, and a 30-day risk-free trial. Support is entirely Canadian.

For business users, the catalogue includes dedicated fibre connectivity, private networks between locations, business voice and collaboration, cloud connect, colocation, and dark fibre. In June 2026, the business announced agreements with Uniti to increase cross-border connectivity between Canada and the United States.

4. Vidéotron Business — Montréal, Québec

*Best for: Quebec businesses wanting internet, mobile and TV from one provider**

Vidéotron has served Quebec since 1964. As a wholly owned subsidiary of Quebecor, it served 1,739,300 internet subscribers as of June 2026 and is now Canada’s fourth wireless provider, with over 4.48 million mobile connections.

Vidéotron provides specialized solutions in fibre, wireless, cloud, and IoT, and the consolidation case is compelling: a Quebec business can manage its internet, mobile fleet, phone service, and television from a single provider, account, and French-language support team. The Helix platform offers symmetrical speeds of up to 2.5 Gbps where infrastructure allows, along with smart Wi-Fi equipment and network management tools.

Helix is coming to Trois-Rivières, Salaberry-de-Valleyfield, Huntingdon, Drummondville, Magog, Rimouski, and Saint-Hyacinthe between 2025 and 2026, followed by municipalities throughout Saguenay-Lac-Saint-Jean. In October 2026 Vidéotron expanded its wireless region into Abitibi-Témiscamingue, Nord-du-Québec, Saguenay-Lac-Saint-Jean, and Bas-Saint-Laurent.

5. Eastlink Business — Halifax, Nova Scotia

*Best for: Atlantic Canadian businesses and multi-location operations**

Eastlink is a family-owned technology and communications firm formed by the Bragg family in 1969 and headquartered in Halifax. With approximately 1,300 employees, it provides internet, mobile, TV, phone, and data services across seven provinces and Bermuda.

Along with business internet and Wi-Fi, available with eero-based or Cisco Meraki managed options, Eastlink Business provides dedicated fibre internet with symmetrical bandwidth of up to 100 Gbps, managed SD-WAN for businesses with multiple locations, cloud connectivity, Ethernet and wavelength services, SIP trunking and voice, business mobile, and colocation at its Pennant Point Data Center.

In June 2026, Eastlink began providing internet service in Moncton, Fredericton, Saint John, Miramichi, Tracadie, and Bathurst, New Brunswick, as well as St. John’s, Newfoundland. In Atlantic Canada, being able to walk into a store and talk to someone in your community remains a significant advantage.

At a Glance

  • TELUS Business (Vancouver, BC): Western Canada and parts of Quebec — PureFibre with Business Wi-Fi and wireless failover backup.
  • SaskTel (Regina, SK): Saskatchewan, urban and rural — infiNET up to 5 Gbps for business, plus cybersecurity bundles.
  • Beanfield (Toronto, ON): Toronto, Montréal, Vancouver, Ottawa — independently owned fibre; unlimited, no contract, price guarantee.
  • Vidéotron Business (Montréal, QC): Quebec and parts of Eastern Ontario — Helix to 2.5 Gbps symmetrical; internet, mobile and TV in one place.
  • Eastlink Business (Halifax, NS): Atlantic Canada and seven provinces — dedicated fibre to 100 Gbps, SD-WAN and colocation.

What to Ask Before You Sign

Begin with the upload speed rather than the download. A small business sending video files, running cloud backups, hosting video calls, or running a VoIP phone system is limited by the upload — which is why symmetrical fibre is worth paying for.

Then ask three questions the leaflet does not answer. What happens if it goes down — is there a service commitment, expected restoration time, and automated wireless failover? Who answers the phone at 7 a.m., and is business support in a separate queue? What is the renewal rate after the promotional period ends? If you accept payments on-site, price a backup connection at the same time; it usually costs less than one lost afternoon of sales.

Finally, confirm your exact address with multiple providers because availability varies by building.

building-a-small-business-foundation-tod.title: Building a Small Business Foundation Today for Growth Tomorrow
building-a-small-business-foundation-tod.author: CanadianSME
building-a-small-business-foundation-tod.alt: Building a Small Business Foundation Today for Growth Tomorrow
building-a-small-business-foundation-tod.excerpt: Anthony Chiotis of ADP Canada on payroll foundations, investing in people and building a trusted partner network.
building-a-small-business-foundation-tod.html:
By Anthony Chiotis, Director Implementation, HR Tech, ADP Canada

If you ask most small business owners what inspired them to start their business, the answer is rarely payroll, compliance, or administration. More often, it’s a passion they wanted to share, a problem they wanted to solve, or a community they wanted to serve. That passion fuels innovation, creates stronger customer relationships, and inspires employees to rally behind a shared purpose.

But passion alone doesn’t build a sustainable small business.

Behind every successful small business are hours of unseen work that keep operations running. Between scheduling, compliance, recruiting, and people management, small business owners often find themselves sticking around well after the doors close. In fact, ADP Research’s Today at Work found that 17% of workers at Canadian small businesses reported putting in 6 to 15 hours of unpaid work each week, while another 12% reported putting in 16 or more.

One of the most important aspects of running a small business is payroll. Payroll touches nearly every part of a business, from employee trust and compliance to cash flow management and talent retention. Whether hiring a first employee or expanding across provinces, establishing effective payroll practices early creates a foundation that helps businesses grow with confidence.

In honour of Small Business Month in October, ADP Canada released the Payroll Toolkit, a resource designed to support Canadian small business owners navigating common payroll challenges at every stage of growth. Here are three ways owners can build the foundation needed to grow with confidence:

Build a Strong Payroll Foundation

Businesses that establish a payroll foundation early benefit from a strong organizational structure. From registering with the Canada Revenue Agency and collecting employee information to establishing pay schedules and tracking statutory requirements, a sound payroll process from the beginning reduces risk and creates consistency as an organization grows.

Payroll technology and AI automation have also transformed some of these tasks from administrative necessities into strategic growth enablers. When automation reduces manual work, automates calculations and streamlines record keeping, it helps avoid costly errors. According to ADP’s Potential of Payroll survey, 29% of payroll leaders globally say adopting AI into payroll is a key driver of transforming their operations.

As workforce complexity increases, the cost of getting payroll wrong rises alongside it. The right systems create the stability needed to focus on strategic priorities and growth.

Invest in Your People

Once a payroll foundation is in place, growth becomes less about processes and more about people.

For many small businesses, their greatest competitive advantage is their people. According to ADP Canada’s Happiness@Work Index, 84% of workers at Canadian small businesses strongly agree that they can see the impact their work has on organizational success.

Today’s workers want more than a paycheque. They want opportunities to develop new skills and prepare for the future of work. ADP Research found that only 18% of Canadian small business workers feel their employer invests in the skills they need to advance. Stretch assignments, mentorship and AI skills training help employees build capabilities while continuing to drive the business forward.

Establish a Trusted Partner Network

One of the hidden challenges of small business growth is deciding which responsibilities should remain internal and which can be entrusted to experts. Scaling isn’t about doing more work individually but building systems that let owners focus where they create the most value.

Outsourcing HR and payroll to a trusted provider can meaningfully reduce administrative burden and free up time for planning and innovation. According to ADP’s Potential of Payroll survey, 77% of organizations globally say it would be highly valuable to partner with a single provider for HR, payroll, and time management.

Max Li, owner of three Canadian small businesses — Maple Jiu-Jitsu, Richmond Hill Jiu-Jitsu, and Code Ninjas Woodbridge — said partnering with a payroll provider has helped streamline operations.

“Having a trusted payroll provider allows business owners to spend less time working in the business and more time working on it, while benefiting from the accuracy, consistency, and accountability that come with dedicated professional support.” — Max Li

Building a small business will always come with hidden costs, but they don’t have to come at the expense of growth. By investing in the right systems, putting people first, and connecting with trusted partners, owners can reduce administrative complexity and build a strong foundation for the future.

Shaping the future of work with practical solutions for small businesses

Small businesses across Canada face a multitude of challenges. Finding and hiring the right talent can be costly and time-consuming, especially when job postings don’t reach the right audience. The continuous introduction and evolution of new technology can be difficult to understand and absorb, leaving smaller organizations at risk of being left behind.

Magnet, based at Toronto Metropolitan University, is a centre of innovation dedicated to helping employers, workers, and communities adapt to a rapidly changing economy. Through partnerships with industry, governments, post-secondary institutions, and workforce organizations, Magnet develops practical solutions that help businesses adopt emerging technologies, strengthen workforce capability, and improve productivity. Its work focuses on building the adaptive capacity organizations need to compete and grow in an increasingly AI-enabled economy.

With an emphasis on collaboration and digital technology, Magnet offers small businesses a wealth of opportunities to strengthen their resilience and readiness.

Student Work Placement Program

*Access up to $5,000 to help cover the costs of student work placements**

Magnet has been a delivery partner of the Student Work Placement Program (SWPP) since 2019. Funded by the Government of Canada, SWPP offers Canadian employers a wage subsidy of up to $5,000 for each eligible post-secondary student they hire. Students gain early work experience in their field, and employers bring new skills and fresh ideas to their team.

Magnet offers a streamlined application process where employers can target one job posting to 120+ post-secondary job boards across Canada rather than posting on multiple boards. Thousands of employers have already used SWPP to test long-term hires and boost their capacity.

Check eligibility and apply for SWPP funding ↗

Practical AI and Digital Upskilling for SMEs

Through its connection to TMU and multi-sector partnerships, Magnet facilitates learning, networking, and upskilling opportunities for businesses, backed by expert research and experience. Current initiatives include:

  • AI Stewardship Practice (AISP): a six-week facilitated learning experience that develops the practical leadership organizations need to make informed decisions about AI adoption. Join as an individual in a cross-sector cohort, or bring up to seven participants from your own organization.
  • MagnetAI: free upskilling courses to boost your team’s understanding of and confidence in AI adoption, including SME-specific courses and a catalogue of 60+ Skills Bridge courses from the Ontario Chamber of Commerce in AI, cybersecurity, team management, finance and more.

Start learning with MagnetAI ↗

Hear From the Leaders Shaping the Future of Work

  • The Magnet Network Live (MNL) Show: hosted by Mark Patterson, exploring the forces reshaping how Canada works, learns, and competes. Season 2, focused on adapting to uncertainty, features guests from the Ontario Chamber of Commerce, People for Education, Excellence in Manufacturing Consortium and Trucking HR Canada.
  • Adaptive Leaders Podcast: hosted by Mark Patterson and Dr. Lev Gonick of Arizona State University, asking decision-makers how they’re managing a sustained period of technological and workforce change.
