ingaged-creative-productions-growing-thr.author: CanadianSME
ingaged-creative-productions-growing-thr.alt: Ingaged Creative Productions: Growing Through Creativity, Connection, and Community
ingaged-creative-productions-growing-thr.excerpt: An Indigenous-owned company bringing creative services and event production together, while building opportunities for clients, artists and a growing team.
ingaged-creative-productions-growing-thr.html:
An Indigenous-owned company bringing creative services and event production together, while building opportunities for clients, artists, and a growing team.

A conference begins long before anyone steps onto a stage. It needs a purpose, an identity, communications that reach the right people, and a plan for bringing them together. When the doors open, the design, technology, and logistics must all work hand in hand to create a seamless experience.

Ingaged Creative Productions has grown by connecting those pieces.

Founded in 2019, Ingaged Creative Productions has a head office in Fort William First Nation and operates in neighbouring Thunder Bay, Ontario. It has developed into an integrated creative and event production company with 27 team members, supporting more than 100 events each year. Its capabilities span design, website development, marketing, communications, audiovisual production, print, custom products and event management.

Across that work, the approach is consistent: understand what clients are trying to accomplish, bring the right people and resources together, and build relationships that continue beyond delivery.

Services That Grow Together

Ingaged’s expansion has come through developing complementary services. Creative work informs event production; events create opportunities for print, multimedia communications, and web development; artist partnerships bring original work into projects across the company.

For a client, that can mean working with one team from the initial concept through branding, registration, participant communications, printed materials and technical delivery. The same creative direction can carry through an invitation, a stage screen, and a delegate’s take-home materials.

The company supports live, virtual and hybrid events, alongside standalone creative and communications projects. Its work has taken the team across Northwestern Ontario and into other parts of the province, while maintaining its home base in Fort William First Nation.

Investing in Capacity and People

Ingaged has established dedicated teams in design, event services, audiovisual services, and print and production, supported by department leads and shared project management processes. Investments in equipment, transportation and production capabilities have helped the company take on more complex work.

Many employees joined without previous industry experience and built their skills through practical work, training and collaboration. Some who joined in entry-level roles now lead departments, helping newer team members develop their own expertise.

Indigenous Partnerships Within the Business Model

Ingaged’s Indigenous ownership shapes how it works and where it invests. Anishinaabe values of reciprocity, storytelling and lasting relationships inform its approach to clients, colleagues and collaborators.

The Ingaged Creative Marketplace makes those commitments tangible. Through partnerships with 12 Indigenous artists, the company develops products featuring licensed artwork, with royalties paid to the artists on sales. Licensed artwork can also appear in conference identities, annual reports, signage, custom gifts and stage displays.

Ingaged also works with Indigenous entrepreneurs, performers, translators, crafters, and Knowledge and Language Keepers — bringing expertise and cultural understanding into projects while directing business opportunities toward the people and communities contributing to them.

A Place for the Next Stage of Growth

Ingaged purchased and renovated a historic community hall in Thunder Bay’s Simpson Street neighbourhood. Built in 1890, it had served the community for generations before falling into disrepair. Ingaged transformed it into The Outset, an events venue that continues the building’s tradition as a gathering place while bringing the company’s creative, technical, and event services together under one roof.

Its work also includes gatherings with significance well beyond production. Ingaged has co-delivered the Neeganii-Iishawin Gathering, one of the largest annual Indigenous gatherings in the region, and supported the Children of Shingwauk Alumni Association Gathering, where residential school Survivors and their families come together.

For Ingaged, the next stage of growth builds on the connections already at the heart of the company: between creative disciplines, between clients and audiences, and between commercial activity and community opportunity.

lemon-lily-tea-brings-natural-flavours-a.title: Lemon Lily Tea Brings Natural Flavours and Sustainable Innovation to Canadian Tea Lovers
lemon-lily-tea-brings-natural-flavours-a.cat: UPS Small Business of the Day
lemon-lily-tea-brings-natural-flavours-a.author: CanadianSME
lemon-lily-tea-brings-natural-flavours-a.alt: A Lemon Lily tea pouch in front of colourful cocktails on a beach, and a box set of Lemon Lily tea pouches and a jar of Lux.
lemon-lily-tea-brings-natural-flavours-a.excerpt: Founded in Toronto in 2012, family-owned Lemon Lily Tea has built a 200-blend business on natural ingredients, responsible sourcing and measurable sustainability.
lemon-lily-tea-brings-natural-flavours-a.html:
As Canadians grow more concerned about what’s in their daily beverages and the environmental impact of their purchases, Lemon Lily Tea offers a solution that blends quality, natural ingredients, and sustainability. Founded in 2012 in Toronto, this family-owned Canadian tea company has built its reputation on handcrafted loose-leaf teas, inventive flavour combinations, and a commitment to responsible sourcing. Lemon Lily, with over 200 tea kinds and a growing presence in Canada and the United States, shows how a desire to make better choices can build a successful Canadian business.

A Canadian Tea Company Built on Passion and Purpose

Entrepreneur Jason Johnston launched Lemon Lily Tea in 2012 after seeing an opportunity to make tea products without artificial flavourings or unnecessary additives. Inspired by his tea experiences and growing interest in natural ingredients, Johnston spent significant time researching tea estates, ingredient sources, and blending methods before creating the company’s line. His vision was straightforward. Tea should taste great while retaining the natural properties of its ingredients.

Lemon Lily prioritized ingredient quality, transparency, and unique flavour characteristics over competing on price. This attitude became the cornerstone of a company that now sells hundreds of tea blends made from ingredients sourced worldwide. Johnston’s entrepreneurial career exemplifies the commitment required to establish an independent Canadian food and beverage brand. In his published anniversary thoughts, he recalled the company’s early financial challenges and uncertainty, highlighting the value of tenacity, family support, and customer loyalty.

More Than 200 Tea Varieties for Every Preference

One of Lemon Lily’s distinguishing features is the breadth of its product line. The company sells over 200 teas and herbal infusions, appealing to both traditional mixes and those looking to try new flavours. Its offerings include traditional black teas, green teas, herbal infusions, fruit teas, matcha, and naturally caffeine-free choices. Lemon Lily also provides superfood powders, hot chocolate, and customized beverage mixes. Its unique offerings include Canadian Maple Earl Grey, Unicorn Sparkles, and Reishi Hot Chocolate. These items demonstrate the brand’s interest in blending recognizable components with unique flavour combinations.

For consumers who like classic tea experiences, the company also provides Japanese Hojicha, Earl Grey, and English Breakfast. Lemon Lily’s teas are handcrafted and brewed fresh to order in its Toronto facility, ensuring product freshness and quality.

Natural Ingredients and a Commitment to Quality

Lemon Lily’s product philosophy focuses on natural ingredients while avoiding artificial flavours, colours, and genetically modified ingredients. The brand says its teas are gluten-free, nut-free, and vegan, with ingredients sourced from organic tea plantations and farms. Instead of synthetic flavourings, the blends use fruits, herbs, spices, natural extracts, and plant-derived oils. A key distinction involves organic certification. Lemon Lily previously held organic certification from 2013 to 2021, but elected not to renew it. According to its official FAQ, the company continues to source from certified organic farms despite no longer holding company-level accreditation.

This strategy represents the brand’s commitment to ingredient sourcing and product transparency. It also emphasizes the need to distinguish between items made with organically sourced ingredients and those with active organic certification.

Advancing Sustainability Through Measurable Environmental Initiatives

Environmental responsibility is another key aspect of Lemon Lily’s business. The corporation has implemented measures to reduce carbon emissions, packaging waste, and energy use, and to manage resources responsibly. Lemon Lily announced a partnership with Greenspark, an environmental impact platform, in May 2024. Under the agreement, the corporation agreed to fund carbon removal, tree planting, ocean kelp restoration, and plastic recovery efforts in response to consumer orders. Lemon Lily announced several environmental goals in its March 2025 sustainability statement.

Company-reported environmental impact figures published in March 2025:

  • 36 tonnes of carbon removal funded
  • 4,000 trees planted
  • 400 ocean kelp plants supported
  • 11,000+ plastic bottles recovered

The company also claims it recycles 99% of its operating waste and reuses roughly 95% of inbound shipment boxes for wholesale deliveries. Although Lemon Lily touts its overall goal of becoming climate-positive, its March 2025 report explicitly said the business has achieved carbon neutrality through environmental activities. These environmental claims are self-reported, not independently validated, measurements of the company’s total operational footprint. Together, these efforts show how Canadian small businesses can incorporate environmental concerns into their daily operations and customer interactions.

Expanding Across Canada and the United States

Since its inception in 2012, Lemon Lily Tea has grown beyond its Toronto roots, establishing partnerships with retailers, cafés, restaurants, spas, and other hospitality enterprises. According to the company’s official website, it sells its teas and superfood powders at over 900 locations in Canada and the United States. Lemon Lily also offers wholesale services, private-label products, and custom tea blends for businesses looking to add natural teas to their offerings. These services enable independent merchants, restaurants, and wellness enterprises to offer specialty tea items to their customers. This growth highlights opportunities for Canadian businesses that combine product differentiation with a strong commitment to quality and customer service.

Celebrating 14 Years of Tea Innovation and Recognition

Lemon Lily will celebrate its 14th year in business in 2026, marking the transition from an entrepreneurial idea to a well-established Canadian tea brand. The company’s official website emphasizes its history of industry acclaim, noting that newspapers, associations, and festivals have honoured its teas for more than a decade. Lemon Lily also claims an average customer rating of 4.9 stars from over 4,000 customers. Its current product lines reflect ongoing innovation, with featured collections including ceremonial matcha, micro-ground powders, quick beverage blends, and seasonal autumn teas.

The brand has also received media attention. Its official wholesale website includes appearances and features on Breakfast Television, The Marilyn Denis Show, CTV Morning Live, Toronto Life, Canadian Living, and Today’s Parent. While these accolades reflect the company’s existing presence, we could not reliably validate any newly bestowed honours for 2025 or 2026.

Bringing People Together One Cup at a Time

Beyond its expanding product variety and sustainability efforts, Lemon Lily Tea shows how modest daily routines can shape important moments. Whether enjoyed as part of a morning routine, shared during a discussion, or served in a café, tea offers a chance to unwind and connect. Lemon Lily encourages people to evaluate the quality and origins of the products they consume by using natural ingredients, creative blends, and responsible business practices. For Canadian entrepreneurs, the company’s journey exemplifies how an independent corporation may pursue economic success while upholding its original principles and environmental responsibilities.

Discover the Natural Flavours of Lemon Lily Tea

Lemon Lily has a broad range for clients eager to discover natural flavours, including traditional loose-leaf teas and herbal infusions, matcha, and novel superfood powders. Experience the quality and originality of Canadian-made tea while also supporting a company dedicated to ethical sourcing and sustainability. Visit www.lemonlily.ca to browse Lemon Lily’s entire tea selection, try new blends, and find your next favourite cup.

park-fifth-co-redefining-canadian-occasi.title: Park & Fifth Co: Redefining Canadian Occasion Wear with Timeless Elegance and Sustainable Fashion
park-fifth-co-redefining-canadian-occasi.cat: UPS Small Business of the Day
park-fifth-co-redefining-canadian-occasi.author: CanadianSME
park-fifth-co-redefining-canadian-occasi.alt: A clothing boutique with racks of dresses on the left, and a bride with her bridesmaids holding bouquets on the right.
park-fifth-co-redefining-canadian-occasi.excerpt: How Vancouver-based Park & Fifth Co is reinventing bridesmaid, bridal and occasion wear with Canadian production, deadstock fabrics and B Corp certification.
park-fifth-co-redefining-canadian-occasi.html:
Learn how Vancouver-based Park & Fifth Co is reinventing wedding apparel, bridesmaid dresses, and special occasion attire with intelligent design, Canadian artistry, and a dedication to sustainability. Fashion matters most when the pieces we wear are meant for life’s special occasions. Park & Fifth Co is a Canadian fashion brand offering a fresh take on women’s eventwear, with contemporary silhouettes, carefully chosen fabrics, and versatile patterns. Founded in Vancouver in 2016, the company has built a distinct identity in the Canadian fashion industry by creating dresses that feel elegant beyond a single occasion.

Park & Fifth blends timeless design with practical versatility, offering everything from modern bridesmaid dresses and minimalist bridal collections to stylish wedding guest attire and everyday occasion wear. Its strategy focuses on quality, responsible manufacturing, and apparel women feel comfortable wearing again and again.

From a Vancouver Studio to a Canadian Fashion Brand

Park & Fifth started in a small workshop in Vancouver’s Gastown neighbourhood in 2016 with a simple goal: to rethink classic bridesmaid dresses. The founders realized bridesmaid dresses were often bought for a single event and rarely worn again. Rather than following traditional bridal fashion expectations, the brand created contemporary styles that could be worn beyond weddings to other important occasions. Brooke and Zoe, the brand’s co-owners, have established Park & Fifth’s recognizable aesthetic by emphasizing design, fit, and conscientious production.

Park & Fifth has grown beyond its Vancouver roots, serving an international clientele from studios in Vancouver, Toronto, and Calgary. Its growth reflects the growing need for occasion wear that balances modern design, comfort, and long-term wardrobe value.

The Un-Bridesmaid Collection: Dresses Designed to Be Worn Again

One of Park & Fifth’s signature items is the Un-Bridesmaid Collection, created on the premise that bridesmaid dresses should be wearable long after the wedding. The collection offers a wide range of colours, shapes, and fabrics, letting wedding parties coordinate their looks while honouring unique preferences. Customers can choose from satin, satin jacquard, crepe, and chiffon dresses in lengths ranging from midi to floor-length. Popular colour families include champagne, sage green, blue, lavender, burgundy, and classic black.

The designs include a variety of necklines, supportive bodices, and lengths to suit different wedding venues and personal style. Park & Fifth also offers up to six complimentary fabric swatches, making it easy to compare fabrics and harmonize wedding colour palettes before making a purchase. The Un-Bridesmaid Collection challenges the idea that brides should wear their apparel only once.

The White Collection: Modern Bridal Fashion with a Personal Touch

Park & Fifth entered bridal apparel in August 2019 with a dedicated bridal line. Originally based on mix-and-match designs, the range expanded to include stocked bridal pieces, offering buyers more options when selecting wedding apparel. The company’s 2026 White by Park & Fifth collection celebrates modern romanticism with minimalist shapes, beautiful details, and delicate fabrics. Featured designs include the Beaumont Dress, Alexandra Dress, Anya Dress, and Maxwell Mini, and bridal accessories like the Liberty Veil and Eloise Gloves complete the look.

The collection underscores the brand’s focus on versatile bridal wardrobes, with pieces suitable for engagement parties, rehearsal dinners, wedding ceremonies, receptions, and honeymoons. Rather than focusing just on traditional wedding gowns, Park & Fifth designs a diverse range of contemporary bridal fashions for various occasions and personal preferences.

Everyday Elegance Through the Social Occasions Collection

While Park & Fifth built its reputation on bridesmaid dresses, its Social Occasions Collection exemplifies the brand’s broader approach to women’s wear. The collection contains outfits appropriate for wedding guests, dinner parties, graduations, and other social occasions. The company combines feminine designs with modern tailoring to create versatile pieces that can be dressed up or down. Deadstock fabrics are central to the collection. Park & Fifth aspires to eliminate material waste by using leftover textiles that would otherwise go unused, while also creating limited-edition designs. This approach combines the company’s aesthetic vision with its sustainability goals, encouraging customers to invest in items that last beyond seasonal trends.

Commitment to Sustainability and Responsible Canadian Production

Since its inception, Park & Fifth has prioritized sustainability as a core value. According to the company’s official sustainability report, its policies include paying fair salaries to trained garment workers, buying deadstock textiles, recycling fabric offcuts, and collaborating with production partners who share its commitment to responsible manufacturing. According to Park & Fifth, they make most of their clothing in and around Vancouver in small batches, which helps foster partnerships with local manufacturers and allows greater involvement in the production process. Its emphasis on manufacturing clothing for repeated use promotes a more deliberate approach to fashion consumption.

A Major Milestone: B Corp Certification in 2026

One of Park & Fifth’s most significant recent achievements is the declaration that it would become a Certified B Corporation in 2026. The accreditation is linked to requirements for social and environmental performance, accountability, and openness. This milestone reflects Park & Fifth’s ongoing efforts to embed ethical business practices across garment design, material sourcing, manufacturing, and company operations.

The brand characterizes the accreditation as a commitment to continuing progress rather than the end of its sustainability journey. This development strengthens Park & Fifth’s position as a Canadian fashion company that seeks to reconcile financial success with social and environmental responsibility.

Latest Collections and Developments in 2026

Throughout 2026, Park & Fifth continued to improve its collections and customer experience. Recent website upgrades feature the 2026 White Collection, including sophisticated bridal designs and accessories, along with new additions to the Un-Bridesmaid and Social Occasions categories. The company’s web inventory includes current styles such as the Riviera Dress, Devon Dress, Aurora Dress, and Jameson Set, giving buyers a variety of options for special occasions.

Another major improvement is its expanded coordinated bridesmaid shopping experience. Park & Fifth provides curated colour palettes and fabric swatches, letting clients experiment with complementary combinations without requiring every member of the bridal party to wear the same dress. These improvements show how the brand continues to tailor its collections to individual stylistic preferences and shifting expectations for occasion wear.

Creating Personalized Shopping Experiences Across Canada

Park & Fifth operates three Canadian studios, combining internet shopping with personalized in-person styling services. Customers can browse collections, get fitting advice, and coordinate wedding ensembles at its Vancouver, Toronto, and Calgary locations. The brand offers exclusive appointments for bridesmaids and bridal customers, including access to samples and styling advice.

Customers who can’t visit a physical studio can also take advantage of virtual fits, which expand access to individualized coaching beyond the company’s retail locations. This mix of digital convenience and in-person support underscores Park & Fifth’s commitment to making consumers feel educated and confident throughout their shopping experience.

Fashion Designed for Life’s Most Meaningful Moments

Park & Fifth takes a considered approach to current Canadian fashion, combining attractive design, functional versatility, and responsible manufacture. By designing dresses that work for weddings and other occasions, the firm encourages buyers to reconsider special-occasion attire. Its Vancouver manufacturing partnerships, sustainability initiatives, modern bridal designs, and personalized shopping experiences all contribute to a brand identity rooted in quality and personality.

As Park & Fifth expands, its initial idea remains unchanged: apparel should not just look great for one particular occasion, but also provide possibilities to make new memories. Visit www.parkandfifthco.com to see the bridal collections, bridesmaid dresses, and special occasion apparel.

nanuk-protecting-valuable-gear-with-cana.title: NANUK: Protecting Valuable Gear with Canadian-Made Innovation
nanuk-protecting-valuable-gear-with-cana.cat: UPS Small Business of the Day
nanuk-protecting-valuable-gear-with-cana.author: CanadianSME
nanuk-protecting-valuable-gear-with-cana.alt: A person carrying a black Nanuk shoulder bag next to two Nanuk coolers on sandy terrain.
nanuk-protecting-valuable-gear-with-cana.excerpt: Quebec-made NANUK cases protect cameras, drones, medical kits and industrial gear — and its N-PVD system won a Red Dot Design Award.
nanuk-protecting-valuable-gear-with-cana.html:
When important equipment must travel through rain, dust, collision, harsh terrain, or demanding workplaces, the case that protects it becomes part of the equipment. NANUK, a Canadian brand, built its business on that idea, producing high-performance protection solutions for professionals and adventurers who cannot afford to leave their equipment vulnerable.

NANUK designs and manufactures cases in Quebec and uses them across industries, including photography, filmmaking, drones, industrial applications, emergency response, medical services, military activities, and outdoor leisure. Today, the company is expanding its product portfolio while preserving a uniquely Canadian approach to engineering and manufacturing.

From Canadian Manufacturing to Global Gear Protection

NANUK’s corporate history dates back to 1984, when Plasticase began manufacturing plastic boxes as Resentel Ltd. After ownership changes, the company became Plasticase and began designing, engineering, and manufacturing high-quality injection-moulded cases. As demand grew for more durable waterproof cases for professional users, the business created NANUK as a separate protective-case line. The brand name comes from the polar bear, an animal associated with survival in Canada’s Arctic region. NANUK combines that robustness with its design philosophy: equipment protection built to withstand harsh conditions. Today, NANUK says it makes its hard-sided cases at its Quebec factory, giving the company direct control over production standards and quality.

Protection Engineered for Demanding Conditions

NANUK’s core hard cases are designed for durability, organization, and protection from the elements. Many of the company’s cases carry an IP67 rating, protecting against dust and temporary water immersion. NANUK also uses its own NK-7 resin in its hard cases, engineered to withstand collisions and harsh transit conditions. Its industrial solutions undergo testing associated with rigorous transportation and environmental requirements.

NANUK emphasizes testing for impacts, repetitive shocks, vibration, rain, water immersion, and extreme temperatures, and, when appropriate, MIL-STD-810F immersion testing. The cases also include functional design features like the company’s PowerClaw latching system, pressure-management features, changeable foam, padded separators, and wheeled transport options. NANUK backs up its hard cases with a limited lifetime warranty.

Serving Professionals Across Multiple Industries

One of NANUK’s strengths is the wide range of applications its protective gear covers. NANUK provides dedicated camera cases and Pro Photo Kits for photographers and filmmakers to arrange their cameras, lenses, mics, stabilizers, and production equipment. Customizable interiors let professionals tailor the case to a specific equipment setup, rather than forcing valuable gear into a generic storage layout. The business has also created specialized solutions for the fast-growing drone market. Current products include setups for DJI platforms such as the Mavic 4 Pro Creator Combo, Mini 5 Pro Fly More, and other drone systems, along with fitted interiors to organize the aircraft, controllers, batteries, and accessories.

NANUK’s reach stretches far beyond creators. Its portfolio includes cases for first responders, medical professionals, military and law enforcement personnel, industrial technicians, and nature lovers. The company provides EMS and first-aid kits, as well as specialized industrial protection for sensitive equipment. This variety has helped NANUK position itself not only as a case manufacturer but also as an equipment-protection provider that meets specific professional needs.

Moving Beyond the Traditional Hard Case

NANUK’s current portfolio indicates how the company is broadening its definition of equipment protection. Beyond its typical hard cases, the company now sells backpacks, organizers, picture and video bags, outdoor gear, everyday carry solutions, and coolers. Its current product line includes the N-PVD camera and drone ecosystem, N-CUBIK interior organizers, and more outdoor-oriented items such as NANUK coolers. The N-PVD line is especially noteworthy because it brings NANUK’s protection philosophy to soft-sided carrying options. The product features double-layered foam construction, compression-moulded EVA components, adjustable organizational systems, and recycled polyester materials. This expansion lets NANUK support consumers at more points in their journey, from organizing equipment at home to moving it through airports, job sites, and outdoor conditions.

International Recognition for Canadian Design

NANUK’s product design philosophy has also gained international recognition. The NANUK N-PVD Ecosystem has been awarded a Red Dot Design Award for 2024. The internationally known competition assesses performance in areas such as product design, communication design, and design concepts. Red Dot judges emphasized that the N-PVD collection was tailored to regular travellers who need dependable equipment transport.

The system includes a variety of backpack sizes, internal camera units, and technology pouches that combine impact protection, adjustable organization, and ergonomic carrying features. For a Canadian producer competing in the international equipment protection market, the accolade shows how industrial design, alongside durability and performance, can become a key differentiator.

Innovation Built Around What Customers Carry

Protective equipment is becoming more specialized. A filmmaker may carry various camera bodies and lenses, while a drone operator carries batteries, controllers, and aircraft. Emergency responders require quick access to medical equipment, while industrial professionals may demand specialized storage for precision instruments. NANUK addresses these diverse needs with changeable interiors, precision-cut foam, customized panels, branded printing, and colour options for unique uses.

Its bespoke case program transforms a standard protective shell into a purpose-built transportation solution. The combination of physical protection and organization is central to NANUK’s value proposition: equipment should not only survive transport, but also arrive organized and ready to use.

Canadian Protection Designed to Go Anywhere

NANUK’s growth shows how Canadian manufacturing can compete worldwide by specializing in product design and engineering. From tough hard cases to award-winning camera bags, drone protection, medical solutions, and outdoor gear, the firm continues to grow while staying focused on the core dilemma that inspired its origins: protecting expensive equipment where dependability is critical.

For professionals, inventors, and explorers alike, NANUK has elevated the protective case from a simple container to a meticulously designed component of the equipment ecosystem. NANUK.com offers Canadian-made protection products.

larch-wood-canada-crafting-heirloom-kitc.title: Larch Wood Canada: Crafting Heirloom Kitchen Essentials from Cape Breton
larch-wood-canada-crafting-heirloom-kitc.cat: UPS Small Business of the Day
larch-wood-canada-crafting-heirloom-kitc.author: CanadianSME
larch-wood-canada-crafting-heirloom-kitc.alt: A Larch Wood store exterior with an A-frame chalkboard sign, and an interior display of wooden cutting boards.
larch-wood-canada-crafting-heirloom-kitc.excerpt: In East Margaree, Nova Scotia, 22 craftspeople turn Eastern Canadian larch into end-grain cutting boards sold from Halifax to Williams-Sonoma.
larch-wood-canada-crafting-heirloom-kitc.html:
Larch Wood Canada, based in East Margaree on Cape Breton Island, has created a reputation around something increasingly rare in modern manufacturing: unhurried, local production with the assumption that the items will survive. The Nova Scotia company specializes in handcrafted end-grain cutting boards, chopping blocks, countertops, flooring, and other wood items created from Eastern Canadian larch in its Cape Breton plant. Rather than masking the material’s natural variety, Larch Wood incorporates the tree’s texture, colour, and growth patterns into each final item’s design.

From Flooring to Premium Cutting Boards

Larch Wood Enterprises began in 2003, when a small group of carpenters and woodworkers bought a 14,000-square-foot building in Margaree, Nova Scotia. The company initially focused on flooring products, but after about two years, it began exploring other uses for larch. Recognizing the benefits of end-grain construction for kitchen work surfaces, the team created the first small, medium, and large cutting boards. Before bringing the items to market, Larch Wood sent prototype boards to local chefs for six months of practical testing. Positive responses helped verify the design and encouraged the company to enter the cookware market.

Handcrafted on Cape Breton Island

Every Larch Wood cutting board is handcrafted on Cape Breton Island. The company says its staff includes 22 crafters and skilled artisans with over a century of collective woodworking experience. Each person helps with the cutting, drying, milling, arranging, gluing, finishing, and quality-control operations involved in producing the finished product. Larch Wood’s local production style allows them more control over both materials and artistry than enterprises that rely primarily on outsourced manufacturing. Its items aren’t just assembled in Canada. The company processes the wood itself and has created a kiln-drying schedule designed exclusively for Eastern Canadian larch.

Why Eastern Canadian Larch Matters

Larch Wood’s identity is strongly related to Eastern Canadian larch, sometimes known locally as tamarack or juniper. The plant thrives on Cape Breton Island and is recognized for its unusual growth rings, warm natural colouring, durability, flexibility, and rot resistance. Because of these properties, larch has long been utilized in boat building, decking, and fencing. Its combination of strength and flexibility is especially beneficial for cutting boards. Larch Wood employs kiln-dried larch from sustainably managed woodlots in the surrounding area, as well as material supplied by smaller regional woodland owners. The company claims to compensate those suppliers above market value to promote a healthy local forestry economy.

Making End Grain the Centre of the Design

One of the distinguishing qualities of Larch Wood’s products is its end-grain structure. Instead of laying large strips of wood horizontally across the cutting table, end-grain construction reveals the ends of the wood fibres. When a knife contacts the board, the fibres can detach slightly before returning to their original place. This creates what Larch Wood calls a self-healing, knife-friendly surface, which reduces wear on knife edges while also giving the board robustness under repeated cutting. The production approach is more labour-intensive than many traditional cutting-board designs, but it is essential to the company’s reputation for longevity and performance.

Every Board Has Its Own Pattern

Larch Wood does not consider natural variation a defect. Growth ring spacing, knots, mineral-driven colour variations, and grain patterns vary from tree to tree. As a result, no two cutting boards appear alike. The company’s craftspeople purposefully arrange end-grain blocks to highlight these distinctions, creating the circular, flowing, and geometric designs synonymous with the Larch Wood aesthetic. For clients, this means that each board serves as both a culinary utensil and a one-of-a-kind piece of woodwork.

Premium and Standard Lines

Larch Wood now provides both Premium and Standard Line cutting boards. The contrast is primarily cosmetic, rather than functional. Standard Line items may have more evident natural qualities, such as tiny knots or intense colour variations. According to the business, these qualities do not negatively affect the board’s performance, build quality, or lifetime. Both product lines follow the same end-grain principles and are covered by the company’s warranty. This method also allows Larch Wood to make better use of naturally varying timber rather than discarding otherwise functional materials solely for aesthetic reasons.

Built With Longevity in Mind

Larch Wood promotes its cutting boards as “items meant to survive for generations when properly maintained.” The company currently backs its cutting boards with a 10-year limited guarantee covering faults in materials and artistry during regular use. Wood is a natural material; thus, proper maintenance is still necessary. Larch Wood recommends hand washing rather than dishwasher cleaning, avoiding extended water contact, storing boards away from concentrated heat, and treating the wood regularly to prevent drying. This emphasis on upkeep underscores the company’s overall concept of viewing kitchen gadgets as long-term investments rather than disposable home items.

Growing Beyond Cutting Boards

Although cutting boards are the company’s best-known product, Larch Wood’s talents extend far beyond them. Its current product line comprises carving boards, round and square boards, chopping blocks, countertops, floors, stools, serving pieces, and other kitchen and living accessories. The company began offering bespoke countertops in 2012, and demand prompted it to build a specialized custom-workshop facility in 2017. Butch, a professional-grade chopping block intended as a modern take on the old butcher block, is one of the company’s most substantial custom goods.

Recognition Through Major Retail Partnerships

Larch Wood’s products have reached customers far beyond Nova Scotia. After originally promoting their boards in Halifax, the company expanded to Toronto, Montreal, and the US. At its first Toronto trade exhibition, the Museum of Arts and Design in New York and the Gardiner Museum in Toronto purchased items, which the business claims were long-term customers. Larch Wood has also had a trade partnership with Williams-Sonoma for over a decade, indicating a strong support for the company’s craftsmanship in the premium kitchenware industry. Its boards are also currently available from Sur La Table, where they are touted as professional-grade, heirloom-quality, Canadian-made cutting boards.

Recognition Among Kitchen Experts

Larch Wood has long piqued the interest of expert cooks and kitchen product reviewers. The company’s review collection includes coverage from the National Post, which highlighted Larch Wood in a compilation of cutting boards suggested by a knife expert. Professional chef Diesheng Huang also put a Larch Wood round chef’s block through rigorous cleaver testing, reporting high grades for durability and stability after repetitive slicing of meat and bone. While these are not formal awards, they do provide practical third-party certification of the company’s products in rigorous culinary situations.

Supporting Sustainable Local Forestry

Sustainability at Larch Wood begins with sourcing. The company employs a renewable tree species grown locally and sources from the region’s sustainably managed woodlots. Because production takes place on Cape Breton Island, much of the core manufacturing process remains close to the raw material source. Instead of discarding every apparent flaw, the company incorporates natural wood diversity into its Standard Line. Combined with the extended lifespan envisaged for its products, this approach supports a paradigm that prioritizes durability and resource efficiency over rapid replacement.

Canadian Craftsmanship Designed to Endure

More than two decades after its inception, Larch Wood Canada remains inextricably linked to where it began. Its workshop, craftspeople, raw materials, and product identity are all based in Cape Breton. That connection is part of what makes the company unique. In a market dominated by mass-produced kitchen utensils, Larch Wood still relies on skilled local woodworking, responsibly sourced Canadian hardwood, and labour-intensive end-grain construction. The result is a product that will last far longer than a few years in the kitchen. With careful care, a Larch Wood cutting board can become one of those familiar household things that develops character over time and becomes a fixture in the kitchen for years to come.

Consumers looking for Canadian-made cookware that combines performance, natural materials, and traditional craftsmanship will find Larch Wood Canada’s approach to timeless design unusual. Visit larchwoodcanada.com to see Larch Wood Canada’s handcrafted collection.

grynd-building-canadian-sports-nutrition.title: GRYND: Building Canadian Sports Nutrition Around Real Food and Better Fuel
grynd-building-canadian-sports-nutrition.cat: UPS Small Business of the Day
grynd-building-canadian-sports-nutrition.author: CanadianSME
grynd-building-canadian-sports-nutrition.alt: Two pouches of Grynd endurance butter next to a woman eating a Grynd maple sea salt energy waffle.
grynd-building-canadian-sports-nutrition.excerpt: Family-owned GRYND, from Calgary and West Kelowna, fuels 50,000+ athletes with maple-syrup energy waffles sold at 150+ Canadian retailers.
grynd-building-canadian-sports-nutrition.html:
For athletes, nutrition is frequently a practical question. Can food provide energy when needed without hindering training or competition? GRYND, a Canadian sports nutrition firm, is based on a simple idea: create performance fuel with easily identifiable ingredients, such as Canadian maple syrup, and in formats tailored for real-world training. GRYND is a family-owned and operated business with locations in Calgary, Alberta and West Kelowna, British Columbia. The company manufactures sports nutrition products in Canada for runners, cyclists, hockey players, endurance athletes, and everyday active consumers who want accessible alternatives to highly processed performance foods.

Built by Athletes Looking for Better Fuel

GRYND says the company grew out of firsthand involvement in competitive sports. Its team grew up playing sports such as hockey, running, cycling, and baseball, and they knew the frustration of performance nutrition products that either didn’t taste good, were hard to tolerate during exercise, or failed to deliver the desired experience during demanding sessions. Instead of accepting these limits, the team started inventing its own approach to sports nutrition. The result was GRYND, a brand centred on what it defines as clean Canadian fuel, made with ingredients consumers can recognize.

Putting Canadian Maple Syrup at the Centre

Canadian maple syrup is a distinctive feature of GRYND’s product identity. Its organic energy waffles use Canadian maple syrup as a portable carbohydrate source for training, racing, games, and other strenuous activities. Rather than constructing another standard sports bar, GRYND was inspired by the thin stroopwafel style. A Dutch family in Norwich, Ontario, makes the company’s waffles from a traditional stroopwafel recipe passed down through generations. GRYND blends the standard formula with Canadian maple syrup and organic ingredients to create a uniquely Canadian endurance fuel.

Five Flavours for Different Training Days

GRYND’s energy waffle line now includes five maple-inspired flavours. The current product line includes Maple Sea Salt, Maple Saskatoon Berry, Maple Chocolate Strawberry, Maple Raspberry, and Maple Apple Fritter. The Maple Raspberry and Maple Apple Fritter variants are certified gluten-free. Each waffle is individually wrapped and designed to fit easily in running vests, cycling jerseys, gym bags, and other gear athletes use while exercising. Standard waffles contain roughly 20 grams of carbohydrates, making them an ideal portable source of nutrition before or during extended workouts.

A Focus on Recognizable Ingredients

One of GRYND’s key brand statements is ingredient simplicity. Its energy waffles use organic ingredients and contain no artificial sweeteners. Ingredient lists vary by flavour, but the original waffles include organic brown rice syrup, organic sugar, organic maple syrup, organic wheat flour, organic palm oil, organic soy flour, sea salt, organic rice extract, natural maple flavour, soy lecithin, and baking soda. The brand promotes this real-food approach as an alternative for athletes who want to avoid traditional gels, chews, and highly processed sports snacks. Rather than focusing solely on laboratory-style concoctions, GRYND aims to show that familiar foods can also fit into an athlete’s training program.

Going Beyond the Energy Waffle

GRYND is already moving beyond the product that helped build the brand. Its second major product category is Natural Endurance Butter, made with peanuts, honey, chocolate, and MCT oil. The product is offered in 32-gram single-serve containers and 125-gram resealable pouches, and it is marketed as a denser calorie source for long workouts and endurance sports. GRYND also sells bundles that combine waffles and Endurance Butter, giving athletes multiple fueling options based on the time and demands of their exercise.

A Maple Energy Gel Is Coming Next

The company’s next planned expansion takes its Canadian ingredient philosophy into one of sports nutrition’s most important sectors. GRYND says it’s creating a maple syrup-based energy gel with Canadian components. The planned product aims to offer a more natural alternative to typical sports gels. It is part of the company’s broader strategy to develop products for various stages of an athlete’s routine. The company’s future aspirations include goods for before, during, and after activity, as well as potential categories including trail nibbles, protein, and hydration. That direction shows that GRYND is aiming to become more than a single-product snack firm, instead establishing a larger Canadian sports nutrition platform.

Growing to More Than 150 Canadian Retailers

GRYND’s retail footprint has grown significantly since the company’s inception. According to the brand, its items are currently available at over 150 retailers across Canada, including specialty stores, hockey retailers, and other sporting-goods businesses. That physical retail presence is especially crucial in sports nutrition, as players frequently find items through races, training communities, athletic retailers, teammates, and coaches rather than traditional grocery stores. GRYND also sells directly to customers via its Canadian e-commerce website.

Fuelled by More Than 50,000 Athletes

Another significant milestone is the company’s expanding athlete base. GRYND claims that over 50,000 Canadian athletes have utilized its goods for training and competition in the brand’s first two years. Its audience is diverse, including runners, cyclists, hockey players, and endurance athletes. The brand also collaborates with Canadian running clubs, hockey teams, cycling groups, and stores as part of a community-focused growth strategy. Rather than focusing just on elite pros, GRYND typically refers to its target audience as everyday athletes – people who balance sport, job, family life, and other commitments.

Designed for Training in the Real World

Convenience is central to GRYND’s product design. Energy waffles are flat, individually wrapped, and easy to transport while running, cycling, or doing other sports. The business recommends them for a variety of situations involving physical exertion, including before exercise and periodically during lengthier sessions. This focus highlights one of the biggest challenges in sports nutrition. A performance food may have an amazing nutritional profile. Still, if it is difficult to transport, unpleasant to eat during exercise, or inconvenient during a race or game, its practical utility is restricted. GRYND’s strategy therefore focuses equally on usability and nutrition.

Building Sports Nutrition With a Canadian Identity

GRYND’s Canadian identity goes beyond branding. The company was founded in Western Canada, manufactures its energy waffles in Ontario, uses Canadian maple syrup, and distributes its products to Canadian sporting communities and stores. That positioning distinguishes GRYND in a sports nutrition market dominated by huge worldwide brands. Rather than simply reproducing established items, the company blends well-known Canadian ingredients and local production relationships into new products. Another example is the Maple Saskatoon Berry flavour, which combines maple with a berry closely linked to Western Canadian cuisine.

Making Performance Nutrition More Approachable

GRYND’s success reflects a broader shift in consumer attitudes toward sports nutrition. Performance items are no longer limited to professional athletes or marathon runners. Recreational runners, cyclists, hockey players, hikers, gym-goers, and parents with hectic schedules are increasingly turning to handy nutrition items to support their active lifestyles. At the same time, many customers are paying greater attention to ingredient labels and seeking out familiar meals. GRYND is positioned at the crossroads of these two trends: performance-focused convenience and a real-food approach.

The Next Stage of GRYND

With over 150 Canadian retailers, over 50,000 athletes fueled, an expanding five-flavour waffle line, natural Endurance Butter, and a maple energy gel in development, GRYND is creating a strong foothold in Canada’s sports nutrition sector. Its proposition remains basic. Athletes want easy energy, but that doesn’t have to mean sacrificing familiar foods, taste, or a connection to where food comes from. GRYND aims to make everyday performance nutrition feel more like real food by blending Canadian maple syrup, organic ingredients, portable formats, and products based on firsthand sports experience.

That mindset fits a corporation founded on the idea that excellence comes from constant hard work. Your brilliance lies in the GRYND. Grynd.ca offers Canadian-made sports nutrition products.

neferland-creating-smarter-sustainable-p.title: Neferland: Creating Smarter, Sustainable Products for Messy Childhood Moments
neferland-creating-smarter-sustainable-p.cat: UPS Small Business of the Day
neferland-creating-smarter-sustainable-p.author: CanadianSME
neferland-creating-smarter-sustainable-p.alt: A Neferland retail display of baby bibs and smocks, and a toddler wearing an olive-print waterproof smock in a high chair.
neferland-creating-smarter-sustainable-p.excerpt: Engineer and mother Raneem Haddara turned a mealtime problem into Neferland: waterproof bibs and smocks made from recycled bottles.
neferland-creating-smarter-sustainable-p.html:
Childhood is inherently messy. From first foods and finger painting to sensory play and everyday adventures, exploration frequently involves spills, stains, and a lot of clean-up. Neferland, a Canadian children’s brand, has built its business around making crucial moments easier for parents while still letting children explore freely. Raneem Haddara, a mother and engineering PhD, founded the company, which creates items for newborns and young children through practical problem-solving, sustainable materials, safety considerations, and smart design.

A Parenting Challenge That Inspired a Business

Raneem’s first-time parenthood experience inspired Neferland. While on maternity leave with her first kid, she was always washing food stains off her baby’s sleeves after meals. Feeding a child with only a diaper was sometimes offered as an alternative, but it wasn’t realistic in every situation or handy while eating out. Raneem began constructing a long-sleeved bib that may provide more coverage while still looking like an attractive piece of apparel. When other parents asked where they could get one, she realized the problem went beyond her own household. That early solution eventually provided the cornerstone for Neferland.

Where Engineering Meets Parenting

Neferland distinguishes itself by viewing children’s items partially as design problems. According to the company, its items are designed with motor control and child growth in mind, along with the practical issues parents face when eating and playing. Its purpose is to create goods that combine functionality, style, sustainability, and developmental considerations for children’s daily activities. That mindset is evident throughout the bib and smock collection. Rather than limiting the items to meals, Neferland creates them for activities such as painting, baking, water play, crafts, childcare activities, sensory exploration, and other situations where children are encouraged to participate independently.

The Meaning Behind Neferland

The corporate name also symbolizes the idea that underpins the brand. According to Neferland, “Nefer” is an ancient Egyptian word meaning beauty, perfection, and joy. Paired with the fanciful spirit of Neverland, the name creates a brand identity centred on childhood, creativity, pragmatism, and fun exploration. As a result, the firm aims to create functional children’s products that are physically appealing enough to wear as part of an outfit, rather than something parents want to remove right away.

Building Bibs for More Than Mealtime

Waterproof bibs and smocks are the foundation of Neferland’s line. Its current product line includes long-sleeve, short-sleeve, and sleeveless designs, plus the NeferTie, NeferTie 2.0, milestone cards, and several multi-product packages. The brand gathers products for infants, toddlers, and children up to about six years old. Many of its smocks have adjustable neck closures, waist ties, waterproof construction, and pockets to catch spills and food. The brand has both high- and low-pocket options, as well as styles with ornamental elements like ruffles and amusing patterns.

Turning Recycled Bottles Into Everyday Products

Sustainability is another key component of Neferland’s product approach. The company claims its bibs are made from 100% recycled polyester with a waterproof TPU coating. According to Neferland, each bib is made from around eight recycled plastic bottles. Using recycled polyester lets the business combine waste reduction with features especially beneficial for children’s items, such as waterproofing, stain resistance, durability, and ease of washing. The goods are also designed to be wiped clean after minor spills or machine-washed if necessary, allowing for repeated daily use.

Putting Product Safety at the Centre

Parents are understandably concerned about the materials used around newborns and small children. Neferland claims its bibs are OEKO-TEX Standard 100 certified, meaning the tested textiles have been examined for dangerous compounds in accordance with the certification’s requirements. The company prominently displays this certification on several of its current product listings. Raneem sees product safety as inextricably linked to her own parenting viewpoint. In an interview with Shop Local Canada, she underlined the need to develop items free of harmful components, while also being sustainable and functional.

The NeferTie Takes Mess Protection Further

One of the company’s most distinctive products is the NeferTie, a revolutionary coverall-style bib designed to protect more than just a child’s clothing. The product fits around a highchair tray with an adjustable elastic band. It also includes suction cups for smooth dining tables. The goal is to help limit food and spills while letting a child engage more freely at meals at home, in restaurants, or on the go. The current NeferTie is intended for children aged around six months to three years. It is made from recycled polyester and resists water, odours, and stains, as are the company’s other waterproof items.

Supporting Independent Eating and Exploration

Neferland’s approach also closely mirrors the realities of independent eating. Many of the brand’s goods are marketed for baby-led weaning, which encourages youngsters to interact with and investigate food on their own. Independent feeding can help generate valuable learning experiences, but it also invariably results in a mess. Neferland’s products are designed to eliminate the practical friction associated with that process, allowing parents to focus on the child’s pleasure rather than protecting clothing. The same approach applies to art and sensory activities. Neferland positions its smocks as activity wear rather than typical feeding bibs, designing pieces that can handle food, paint, water, and crafts.

Growing the Product Range

Neferland’s current catalogue demonstrates the brand’s expansion beyond its original long-sleeve bib design. Its product line currently includes Every Moment Milestone Cards, sleeveless styles, bundles, the Munchimal, and several variations of the NeferTie. The company has also worked with My Little Eater to offer product bundles that include feeding products, a baby-led feeding course, and a meal plan. This development reflects a broader perspective centred on everyday early childhood experiences rather than a specific product category.

Expanding Canadian Retail Availability

Neferland’s reach has expanded beyond its own direct-to-consumer website. The brand is now available through Well.ca, a Canadian online health and wellness retailer, where Neferland items are offered as solutions designed to support children while making daily feeding and play more convenient for families. Shop Local Canada also profiled Neferland, highlighting the founder’s entrepreneurial path, engineering expertise, commitment to sustainability, and approach to product creation. These placements increase visibility for an independent Canadian children’s brand competing in a market dominated by much larger multinational corporations.

Building a Canadian Brand for the Future

Neferland has also taken steps to safeguard and potentially expand its brand identification. According to Canadian government trademark records, the NEFERLAND trademark application was filed in May 2024 and published in Canada’s Trademarks Journal in September 2025. The application has sections for baby blankets, bibs, children’s apparel, footwear, swimwear, sleepwear, toys, and other baby and children’s goods. While a trademark filing does not guarantee that all these products will be released, the application’s scope shows the range of categories officially connected with the Neferland brand.

Making Everyday Parenting a Little Simpler

Neferland’s story shows how an ordinary parenting dilemma can become the foundation for creative product development. What began as one mother regularly wiping food-covered sleeves has grown into a Canadian firm that produces waterproof, reusable, recycled-material goods based on the challenges of raising young children. Neferland’s concept is grounded in practical design rather than needless complexity, drawing on Raneem Haddara’s engineering expertise and firsthand parenting experience.

For families, this means products that let kids eat, create, experiment, and get messy while making the inevitable cleanup a little easier. Making place for that mess in a child’s environment, where discovery typically occurs through touching, tasting, spilling, painting, and exploring, may be one of the simplest ways to make room for learning. Discover Neferland’s selections at neferlandkids.com.

article.title: Ontario: A Diverse Economy Powered by Entrepreneurship

ps: Ontario brings together established industries, growing technology communities and small businesses serving customers locally and internationally. From Toronto’s financial and professional services sector to manufacturing centres, agricultural communities and northern resource industries, the province offers entrepreneurs a broad range of markets and opportunities.

Small and medium-sized businesses are an essential part of Ontario’s economy. Independent retailers, manufacturers, technology companies, construction firms, hospitality operators and professional service providers contribute to employment, strengthen local supply chains and support communities across the province.

Ontario’s business landscape varies considerably by region. Toronto and the Greater Toronto Area bring together finance, technology, media and professional services. Ottawa has strengths in technology, telecommunications and businesses serving government. Waterloo Region is known for its technology and startup community, while Hamilton and southwestern Ontario have deep roots in manufacturing, automotive production, logistics and agriculture.

Northern Ontario supports businesses in mining, forestry, tourism and related services. Across smaller cities and rural communities, entrepreneurs create opportunities through food production, retail, skilled trades, hospitality and locally delivered services.

Ontario’s urban centres, diverse population, postsecondary institutions and connections to Canadian and U.S. markets provide a foundation for business development. Entrepreneurs can find opportunities in digital services, advanced manufacturing, cybersecurity, clean technology, healthcare services and products that meet the needs of different communities.

Business growth also comes with challenges. Operating costs, access to financing, hiring and competition require careful planning. For small businesses, building strong customer relationships, improving productivity and adapting to changing market conditions are central to long-term success.

Small and medium-sized businesses employ a large share of Quebec’s private-sector workforce, from manufacturers in the regions to creative studios, food producers and service firms in Montréal and Quebec City.

Greater Montréal is a hub for aerospace, artificial intelligence, video games, life sciences and finance. Quebec City has strengths in insurance, optics, digital technology and public-sector services. The Eastern Townships, Centre-du-Québec and Chaudière-Appalaches support manufacturing and agri-food, while the Saguenay–Lac-Saint-Jean and Côte-Nord regions are anchored by aluminum, forestry and mining.
Low-cost hydroelectricity, a strong co-operative and credit-union tradition and regional development networks help businesses outside the major cities.

Opportunities exist in clean energy, electrification of transport, digital services, food processing and tourism. Firms that serve customers well in French gain access to a loyal market and to other francophone markets abroad.
Labour shortages, compliance with French-language and privacy requirements, and the extra administration of a separate provincial tax system are the main planning points for owners.

ps: Nova Scotia’s economy is shaped by the sea, its universities and a growing population. Halifax has become one of the faster-growing cities in Atlantic Canada, bringing new customers and talent for small businesses.
Fishing and seafood companies, tourism operators, retailers, trades firms and technology start-ups employ Nova Scotians in every region.

Halifax concentrates defence and shipbuilding, ocean technology, financial services, health care and higher education. The South Shore and Annapolis Valley are known for seafood, wine, agriculture and tourism. Cape Breton supports tourism, culture and energy, and the Northumberland Shore combines manufacturing and fisheries.
Port of Halifax connections to Europe and the U.S. East Coast support exporters.
Opportunities include ocean technology, offshore wind and clean energy, seafood exports to Europe and Asia, and health and education services. Lower HST from 2025 helps consumer-facing businesses.
Workforce availability and housing remain challenges. Partnering with universities and settlement agencies can help small employers recruit.

ps: New Brunswick is Canada’s only officially bilingual province, giving its businesses an edge in serving both English- and French-speaking customers. Its location between central Canada, the Atlantic provinces and New England makes it a natural trading crossroads.
Small businesses in forestry, seafood, manufacturing, retail and services employ most of the private-sector workforce.

Moncton is a hub for transportation, logistics and bilingual customer service. Saint John has strengths in energy, port activity and manufacturing. Fredericton combines government, cybersecurity, education and technology. The Acadian Peninsula and northern regions rely on fisheries and forestry.
Proximity to Maine gives many businesses straightforward access to U.S. customers.
Opportunities include cybersecurity, energy innovation, value-added wood and seafood products, and remote service delivery. Newcomers are reshaping local markets and the labour pool.
Smaller local markets and an older population mean growth often depends on exports and digital sales.

ps: Newfoundland and Labrador has a resource-rich economy built on the ocean, mining and energy, and a strong tradition of self-reliant entrepreneurship. Small businesses serve communities spread across a large geography.
Fishing enterprises, tourism operators, contractors, retailers and service firms make up most employers.

St. John’s is the main centre for offshore energy, ocean technology, government, health care and Memorial University. Western Newfoundland supports tourism, forestry and fisheries. Labrador is home to iron ore and nickel mining and hydroelectric development, with Indigenous governments and businesses as key partners.
Many coastal communities depend on seasonal fishing and tourism.
Opportunities include ocean technology, aquaculture, tourism, mining supply and clean energy projects. Unique culture and landscapes support a strong tourism brand.
Distance, transportation costs and population decline in rural areas require careful planning. Digital sales and regional partnerships help firms reach wider markets.

Farms, fisheries, food processors, tourism operators, retailers and service businesses form the core of the Island economy.

Charlottetown is the centre for government, health care, bioscience and professional services. Summerside has strengths in aerospace and manufacturing. Rural PEI is known for potatoes, mussels, oysters, lobster and agri-food, and tourism is important everywhere on the Island.
The Confederation Bridge links Island businesses to mainland markets.
Opportunities include bioscience and animal health, food innovation, seasonal and culinary tourism, and services for a growing population.
Seasonality and a small local market mean many firms plan for a busy summer and diversify into exports or year-round services.

Mining exploration and development support suppliers in transportation, camps and equipment. Yukon First Nations, many with modern treaties, are major economic partners.
The Alaska Highway links Yukon to British Columbia and Alaska.
Opportunities include adventure and cultural tourism, mining services, construction and local food production.
High costs, long shipping distances and a small labour pool require careful planning. Northern incentives can help attract staff.

Iqaluit is the centre for government, construction, aviation and retail. Gold and iron ore mines in the Kivalliq and Qikiqtaaluk regions create demand for suppliers. Fisheries for turbot and shrimp operate offshore, and Inuit art and crafts reach markets worldwide.

High costs, limited infrastructure and small markets require long planning horizons and strong community partnerships.

accessibility.title: Accessibility Statement
accessibility.intro: CanadianSME Small Business Magazine, published by Cmarketing Inc., is committed to making our website, magazine, podcast and events accessible to everyone, including people with disabilities. This statement explains the standards we work to, what we do today, where we still have work to do, and how to tell us about a barrier.

ps: Canada’s small business community includes owners, employees and customers with disabilities. We want everyone to be able to read our articles, use our tools, listen to our podcast and take part in our events without barriers. Accessibility is part of how we plan, design, write and publish — not something we add at the end.

We aim to meet the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.1 at Level AA across canadiansme.ca. This is the standard referenced by the Accessibility for Ontarians with Disabilities Act (AODA) Integrated Accessibility Standards, which applies to Cmarketing Inc. as an Ontario organisation. We also follow the principles of the federal Accessible Canada Act: inclusion, dignity, equal opportunity and involving people with disabilities in finding solutions.

sections.h: What we do on this website
items: Use clear headings, landmarks and a logical reading order so screen reader and keyboard users can move through each page.
Write descriptive alternative text for meaningful images, and hide purely decorative images from assistive technology.
Keep text and interactive elements at a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1, and avoid using colour alone to convey meaning.
Make every link, button, menu and form usable with a keyboard, with a visible focus outline.
Label form fields clearly and explain errors in plain language.
Let pages reflow on phones and when zoomed to 200% without losing content.
Pause moving content such as the featured slider and partner logo strip when you hover over or focus on it.
Write in plain, practical language suited to busy owner-operators.

ps: We are working to provide transcripts for CanadianSME Small Business Podcast episodes and captions for video content. Digital magazine issues are published in a page-flip format; if you need an issue or a specific article in an accessible format, contact us and we will provide it.

The Small Business Summit, Small Business Awards and our other events are held in venues with step-free access. When you register, you can tell us about accessibility needs — such as seating, sign language interpretation, dietary needs or a support person — and we will work with you and the venue to meet them. Support persons attend at no charge.
Despite our efforts, some content may not yet be fully accessible:
items: Some older articles may have images without complete alternative text.
Some PDF guides and older magazine issues may not be fully tagged for screen readers.

Content from third parties — embedded podcast players, partner websites, advertising and sponsored materials — is outside our direct control. We ask partners to meet WCAG 2.1 AA and raise issues with them when we find them.

ps: The site is designed to work with current versions of Chrome, Edge, Firefox and Safari, and with common assistive technologies including JAWS, NVDA, VoiceOver and TalkBack, as well as browser zoom and voice control.

You can ask for any information on this website in an alternative format, such as large print, an accessible document, plain text or a conversation by phone. We will provide it at no cost, as soon as practicable, and work with you to choose a format that suits your needs.
